title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
15.1 The SVD Theorem and Subspace Characterization
Several questions from earlier chapters remain open. The Euclidean norm and the condition number of a matrix were defined by optimization problems that we have not yet evaluated, and the least-squares theory of the referenced section gave a computable solution only for matrices with full column rank. The singular value decomposition (SVD) answers these questions. It separates a linear map into orthogonal input directions, nonnegative scale factors, and orthogonal output directions, and unlike an eigendecomposition it exists for every rectangular matrix \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\).
Geometrically, the SVD shows that every linear map sends the unit sphere in \(\fR^n\) to a hyperellipsoid in \(\fR^m\). The right singular vectors \(\bv_i\) are the orthogonal directions in the domain that are mapped to the semi-axes, the singular values \(\sigma_i\) are the semi-axis lengths, and the left singular vectors \(\bu_i\) are the directions of the semi-axes in the codomain.
We first prove that the SVD exists and use it to identify the four fundamental subspaces. We then compute norms and condition numbers, construct the best low-rank approximation, and solve rank-deficient and regularized least-squares problems. The section ends with the way the SVD is computed in practice.
(Running example: data matrices) In a fitting problem with noisy observations, the singular values rank the directions in parameter space by how strongly the data determine them. Truncation and regularization treat the weakly determined directions differently, and principal component analysis interprets the same decomposition as variance.

title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
NoteTheorem: The Singular Value Decomposition Theorem



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) with \(m \geq n\). There exist orthogonal matrices \(\bU \in \fR^{m \times m}\) and \(\bV \in \fR^{n \times n}\), and a rectangular diagonal matrix \(\bsigma \in \fR^{m \times n}\), such that \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \bU \bsigma \bV^T,
\end{align}
\] where the diagonal entries of \(\bsigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, \sigma_2, ..., \sigma_n)\) are real, non-negative, and sorted in non-increasing order: \[
\begin{align}
\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq ... \geq \sigma_r > \sigma_{r+1} = ... = \sigma_n = 0.
\end{align}
\] The number of strictly positive singular values \(r = \operatorname{rank}(\bA)\) equals the rank of \(\bA\). In dyadic outer-product form, \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i \bu_i \bv_i^T.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Consider the Gram matrix \(\bA^T\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\). Because \((\bA^T\bA)^T = \bA^T\bA\), it is symmetric, and for every \(\bx \in \fR^n\), \(\bx^T(\bA^T\bA)\bx = \|\bA\bx\|_2^2 \geq 0\), so \(\bA^T\bA\) is positive semidefinite.
By the Spectral Theorem (the referenced result), \(\bA^T\bA\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors \(\bv_1, ..., \bv_n \in \fR^{n}\) with corresponding real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq ... \geq \lambda_n \geq 0\). Define the singular values \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i} \geq 0\) for \(i = 1, ..., n\), and let \(r\) denote the number of strictly positive singular values, so that \(\sigma_r > 0\) and \(\sigma_{r+1} = ... = \sigma_n = 0\).
For each index \(i \in \{1, ..., r\}\), define the normalized vectors in \(\fR^m\): \[
\begin{align}
\bu_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i} \bA \bv_i.
\end{align}
\] We verify that \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\}\) form an orthonormal set in \(\fR^m\): \[
\begin{align}
\bu_i^T \bu_j
    =
    \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} (\bA\bv_i)^T (\bA\bv_j)
    =
    \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \bv_i^T (\bA^T\bA\bv_j)
    =
    \frac{\lambda_j}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \bv_i^T \bv_j
    =
    \frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \delta_{ij}
    =
    \delta_{ij}.
\end{align}
\] Using Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization, extend \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\}\) to a complete orthonormal basis \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_m\}\) for \(\fR^m\). Assemble the orthogonal matrices \(\bU = [\bu_1, ..., \bu_m] \in \fR^{m \times m}\) and \(\bV = [\bv_1, ..., \bv_n] \in \fR^{n \times n}\).
Evaluating the \((i, j)\) entry of \(\bU^T\bA\bV\): \[
\begin{align}
(\bU^T\bA\bV)_{ij} = \bu_i^T \bA \bv_j.
\end{align}
\] For \(j \leq r\), \(\bA\bv_j = \sigma_j \bu_j\), so \(\bu_i^T \bA\bv_j = \sigma_j \bu_i^T\bu_j = \sigma_j \delta_{ij}\). For \(j > r\), \(\lambda_j = 0\), so \(\|\bA\bv_j\|_2^2 = \bv_j^T\bA^T\bA\bv_j = 0\), which implies \(\bA\bv_j = \bzero\) and \(\bu_i^T\bA\bv_j = 0\). Thus \(\bU^T\bA\bV = \bsigma\), which gives \(\bA = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\).









NoteTheorem: Thin SVD and the Four Fundamental Subspaces



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) have rank \(r \leq n \leq m\). The thin SVD is \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \bU_1 \bsigma_1 \bV_1^T,
\end{align}
\] where \(\bU_1 \in \fR^{m \times r}\) and \(\bV_1 \in \fR^{n \times r}\) have orthonormal columns, and \(\bsigma_1 = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, ..., \sigma_r) \in \fR^{r \times r}\) has strictly positive entries. The complete singular vectors partition the domain and codomain into the four fundamental subspaces:

Column space (range): \(\mathcal{R}(\bA) = \operatorname{span}\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\} \subset \fR^m\).
Left null space: \(\mathcal{N}(\bA^T) = \operatorname{span}\{\bu_{r+1}, ..., \bu_m\} \subset \fR^m\).
Row space: \(\mathcal{R}(\bA^T) = \operatorname{span}\{\bv_1, ..., \bv_r\} \subset \fR^n\).
Null space (kernel): \(\mathcal{N}(\bA) = \operatorname{span}\{\bv_{r+1}, ..., \bv_n\} \subset \fR^n\).









TipProof





From \(\bA = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\), we have \(\bA\bv_i = \sigma_i \bu_i\) for \(i \leq r\) and \(\bA\bv_i = \bzero\) for \(i > r\). Any \(\bx \in \fR^n\) expands uniquely as \(\bx = \sum_{i=1}^n (\bv_i^T\bx)\bv_i\). Applying \(\bA\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bx = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i (\bv_i^T\bx) \bu_i.
\end{align}
\] This expresses \(\bA\bx\) as a linear combination of \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\}\), proving \(\mathcal{R}(\bA) = \operatorname{span}\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\}\). Furthermore, \(\bA\bx = \bzero\) if and only if \(\bv_i^T\bx = 0\) for all \(i \leq r\), which proves that \(\mathcal{N}(\bA) = \operatorname{span}\{\bv_{r+1}, ..., \bv_n\}\). Repeating the argument for \(\bA^T = \bV\bsigma^T\bU^T\) completes the characterization for \(\mathcal{R}(\bA^T)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(\bA^T)\).

title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
15.2 Norms and Condition Numbers
The induced Euclidean norm of the referenced result is the largest amplification of a unit vector, and the condition number of the referenced result compares the largest and the smallest amplification. Both were defined as optimization problems over the unit sphere. Because orthogonal matrices preserve Euclidean length, the SVD reduces these problems to a diagonal matrix, where they can be solved by inspection.






NoteTheorem: Norms and Condition Numbers from the SVD



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) with \(m\geq n\) have singular values \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n\geq0\). Then \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_2=\sigma_1,
    \qquad
    \min_{\|\bx\|_2=1}\|\bA\bx\|_2=\sigma_n,
    \qquad
    \|\bA\|_F=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2\Big)^{1/2}.
\end{align}
\] If \(\bA\) has full column rank, we define \(\kappa_2(\bA)=\sigma_1/\sigma_n\). The condition number satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\kappa_2(\bA)^2.
\end{align}
\] If \(\bA\) is square and nonsingular, then \(\|\bA^{-1}\|_2=1/\sigma_n\), so \(\kappa_2(\bA)=\|\bA\|_2\|\bA^{-1}\|_2\) agrees with the referenced result.








TipProof





Let \(\bx\) be a unit vector and let \(\by=\bV^T\bx\), which is also a unit vector. Since \(\bU\) preserves Euclidean length, \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx\|_2^2=\|\bU\bsigma\bV^T\bx\|_2^2=\|\bsigma\by\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2y_i^2.
\end{align}
\] The sum is a weighted average of the \(\sigma_i^2\), so it lies between \(\sigma_n^2\) and \(\sigma_1^2\). The upper value is attained at \(\by=\be_1\), that is, at \(\bx=\bv_1\), and the lower value is attained at \(\bx=\bv_n\). These two cases prove the first two identities.
For the Frobenius norm, \(\|\bA\|_F^2=\operatorname{trace}(\bA^T\bA)\) and \(\bA^T\bA=\bV\bsigma^T\bsigma\bV^T\). The trace is invariant under the similarity by \(\bV\), so \(\|\bA\|_F^2=\operatorname{trace}(\bsigma^T\bsigma)=\sum_i\sigma_i^2\).
The factorization \(\bA^T\bA=\bV(\bsigma^T\bsigma)\bV^T\) is itself an SVD of \(\bA^T\bA\) with singular values \(\sigma_1^2\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n^2\). When \(\bA\) has full column rank these are positive, and \(\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\sigma_1^2/\sigma_n^2=\kappa_2(\bA)^2\). Finally, if \(\bA\) is square and nonsingular, then \(\bA^{-1}=\bV\bsigma^{-1}\bU^T\) is an SVD whose largest singular value is \(1/\sigma_n\).









NoteCorollary: Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices



If \(\bA\) is symmetric positive definite, its singular values are its eigenvalues, and \(\kappa_2(\bA)=\lambda_{\max}(\bA)/\lambda_{\min}(\bA)\). If \(\bA=\bL\bL^T\) is the Cholesky factorization of the referenced result, then \(\kappa_2(\bL)=\sqrt{\kappa_2(\bA)}\).








TipProof





By the referenced result, \(\bA=\bQ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bQ^T\) with \(\bQ\) orthogonal and positive diagonal \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\). After the eigenvalues are sorted in decreasing order, this factorization is an SVD, which proves the first claim. For the second, \(\bA=(\bL^T)^T\bL^T\), so the argument in the proof of the referenced result shows that the singular values of \(\bL^T\) are the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(\bA\). Transposition does not change singular values, so \(\kappa_2(\bL)=\kappa_2(\bL^T)=\sqrt{\kappa_2(\bA)}\).



The identity \(\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\kappa_2(\bA)^2\) explains the preference for QR in the referenced section. When the normal equations are formed and solved by a backward stable method, the forward error can be as large as a modest multiple of \(\kappa_2(\bA)^2u\), where \(u\) is the unit roundoff. Householder QR works with \(\bA\) directly, and when the least-squares residual is small its forward error is a modest multiple of \(\kappa_2(\bA)u\) (Higham 2002). For \(\kappa_2(\bA)=10^6\) in double precision, these two estimates are of order \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-10}\).

title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
15.4 Least Squares and Regularization
The least-squares theory of the referenced section characterized every minimizer and the minimum-norm minimizer, but it computed a solution only when \(\bA\) has full column rank. The SVD computes all minimizers in every case. It also shows which components of the solution are sensitive to errors in \(\bb\), and how truncation and Tikhonov regularization modify those components.






NoteDefinition: Moore–Penrose Pseudoinverse



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) have rank \(r\) and thin SVD \(\bA = \bU_1 \bsigma_1 \bV_1^T\). The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of \(\bA\) is \[
\begin{align}
\bA^\dagger = \bV_1 \bsigma_1^{-1} \bU_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{\sigma_i} \bv_i \bu_i^T \in \fR^{n \times m}.
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Least Squares by the SVD



Let \(\bA=\bU\bsigma\bV^T\) have rank \(r\). A vector \(\bx\) minimizes \(\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_2\) if and only if \[
\begin{align}
\bv_i^T\bx=\frac{\bu_i^T\bb}{\sigma_i},\qquad i=1,...,r.
\end{align}
\] The minimum residual norm is \(\big(\sum_{i=r+1}^m(\bu_i^T\bb)^2\big)^{1/2}\), and the unique minimizer of smallest Euclidean norm is \[
\begin{align}
\bA^\dagger\bb=\sum_{i=1}^r\frac{\bu_i^T\bb}{\sigma_i}\,\bv_i.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(\by=\bV^T\bx\) and \(\bc=\bU^T\bb\). Since \(\bU^T\) preserves Euclidean length, \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx-\bb\|_2^2
    =\|\bU^T(\bU\bsigma\bV^T\bx-\bb)\|_2^2
    =\|\bsigma\by-\bc\|_2^2
    =\sum_{i=1}^r(\sigma_iy_i-c_i)^2+\sum_{i=r+1}^m c_i^2.
\end{align}
\] The second sum does not depend on \(\bx\). The first sum vanishes exactly when \(y_i=c_i/\sigma_i\) for \(i\leq r\), which proves the characterization and the value of the minimum. The components \(y_{r+1},...,y_n\) are unrestricted. Because \(\|\bx\|_2=\|\by\|_2\), the norm is smallest when these components are zero, and the resulting vector \(\bx=\bV\by\) is \(\bA^\dagger\bb\).



The coefficient \(\bu_i^T\bb/\sigma_i\) shows how errors in the data enter the solution. If \(\bb\) is replaced by \(\bb+\be\), the component of the minimum-norm solution along \(\bv_i\) changes by \(\bu_i^T\be/\sigma_i\). Directions with small singular values amplify the noise by \(1/\sigma_i\), which is the mechanism behind the ill-conditioning measured by \(\kappa_2(\bA)\). Regularization reduces this amplification by modifying the coefficients for small \(\sigma_i\).






NoteTheorem: Filter Factors for Truncation and Tikhonov Regularization



Let \(\bA\) have rank \(r\) and SVD \(\bA=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i\bu_i\bv_i^T\). For \(k\leq r\), the minimum-norm least-squares solution for the truncated matrix \(\bA_k\) of the referenced result is \[
\begin{align}
\bx_k=\bA_k^\dagger\bb=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{\bu_i^T\bb}{\sigma_i}\,\bv_i.
\end{align}
\] For \(\lambda>0\), the Tikhonov solution of the referenced result is \[
\begin{align}
\bx_\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_i^2+\lambda}\,\frac{\bu_i^T\bb}{\sigma_i}\,\bv_i.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





The truncated matrix \(\bA_k\) has rank \(k\) and SVD \(\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i\bu_i\bv_i^T\), so the referenced result gives \(\bx_k\). For the Tikhonov solution, substitute \(\bA=\bU\bsigma\bV^T\) into the normal equations \((\bA^T\bA+\lambda\bI)\bx=\bA^T\bb\). This gives \[
\begin{align}
\bV(\bsigma^T\bsigma+\lambda\bI)\bV^T\bx=\bV\bsigma^T\bU^T\bb.
\end{align}
\] Multiplying by \(\bV^T\) and solving the diagonal system gives \(\bv_i^T\bx_\lambda=\sigma_i\,\bu_i^T\bb/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda)\), which is zero for \(i>r\). Writing \(\sigma_i/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda)\) as \(\sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda)\) times \(1/\sigma_i\) gives the stated form.



Both regularized solutions multiply the unregularized coefficient \(\bu_i^T\bb/\sigma_i\) by a filter factor. Truncation uses the factor one for \(i\leq k\) and zero for \(i>k\), so it removes the weak directions entirely. Tikhonov regularization uses \(\sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda)\), which is close to one when \(\sigma_i^2\gg\lambda\) and close to \(\sigma_i^2/\lambda\) when \(\sigma_i^2\ll\lambda\). The amplification \(1/\sigma_i\) is therefore replaced by at most \(1/(2\sqrt{\lambda})\), and the transition between kept and damped directions occurs near \(\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda}\). The choice between the two methods, and the choice of \(k\) or \(\lambda\), depends on the noise level in \(\bb\) and on the assumption about the solution discussed after the referenced result.






TipRemark



(Computing the SVD) The proof of the referenced result constructs the SVD from the eigendecomposition of \(\bA^T\bA\), but practical codes do not compute it that way. A backward stable eigensolver applied to \(\bA^T\bA\) computes its eigenvalues with absolute errors of order \(u\sigma_1^2\), so singular values below about \(\sqrt{u}\,\sigma_1\) lose all relative accuracy. Golub and Kahan instead reduce \(\bA\) to an upper bidiagonal matrix \(\bB=\bU_0^T\bA\bV_0\) by applying Householder reflections alternately from the left and from the right (Golub and Kahan 1965). A shifted QR iteration applied implicitly to \(\bB\) then computes the singular values, and standard dense libraries follow this two-phase approach. For a large sparse matrix, the bidiagonal matrix can instead be built one column at a time by a recurrence that uses only products with \(\bA\) and \(\bA^T\). The recurrence is closely related to the Lanczos iteration of the referenced section applied to \(\bA^T\bA\).

text:
15.5 Exercises






WarningExercise




Compute. (Hand computation of full and thin SVD) For \(\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 4 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\):

Compute \(\bA^T\bA\) and find its eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) and orthonormal eigenvectors \(\bv_1, \bv_2\).
Compute \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\) and the left singular vector \(\bu_1 = \frac{1}{\sigma_1}\bA\bv_1\).
Complete \(\{\bu_1\}\) to an orthonormal basis of \(\fR^2\) to find \(\bu_2\).
Write down the full SVD \(\bA = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\) and verify that \(\bU\bsigma\bV^T = \bA\).

Compute. (Truncation versus Tikhonov regularization) Let \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-2},10^{-4})\), let \(\bx_*=(1,1,1)^T\), and let \(\bb=\bA\bx_*+10^{-3}(1,-1,1)^T\).

Compute the least-squares solution \(\bA^{-1}\bb\) and its error \(\|\bA^{-1}\bb-\bx_*\|_2\). Identify the component responsible for the error using the coefficients \(\bu_i^T\bb/\sigma_i\).
Compute the truncated solutions \(\bx_1,\bx_2,\bx_3\) of the referenced result and their errors.
Compute the Tikhonov solutions for \(\lambda=10^{-2},10^{-4},10^{-6}\). For each \(\lambda\), list the three filter factors and explain which components are kept and which are damped.

Compute. (Low-rank error accounting) For a diagonal matrix \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(9,4,1)\), compute the best rank-one and rank-two approximations. Verify both the spectral- and Frobenius-norm errors predicted by the referenced result.
Derive. (Verification of the four Moore–Penrose conditions) Using the thin SVD \(\bA = \bU_1 \bsigma_1 \bV_1^T\) and \(\bA^\dagger = \bV_1 \bsigma_1^{-1} \bU_1^T\), prove algebraically:

\(\bA\bA^\dagger\bA = \bA\).
\(\bA^\dagger\bA\bA^\dagger = \bA^\dagger\).
\((\bA\bA^\dagger)^T = \bA\bA^\dagger\) (orthogonal projector onto \(\mathcal{R}(\bA)\)).
\((\bA^\dagger\bA)^T = \bA^\dagger\bA\) (orthogonal projector onto \(\mathcal{R}(\bA^T)\)).

Compute. (SVD image compression and energy decay) In Python, load a grayscale image as a matrix \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\).

Compute the full SVD using scipy.linalg.svd.
Plot the singular value spectrum \(\sigma_i\) on a semilog scale and the cumulative energy ratio \(E(k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2}\) as a function of \(k\).
Reconstruct the image at ranks \(k \in \{5, 20, 50\}\). Compare memory storage against the original image.

Higham, Nicholas J. 2002. Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms. 2nd ed. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027.

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
16.1 From Power Iteration to Krylov Subspaces
The QR algorithm of the referenced result computes every eigenvalue of a dense matrix in \(O(n^3)\) operations. Many applications instead require a few eigenvalues of a large sparse matrix, and the matrix is often available only through the product \(\bv\mapsto\bA\bv\). Power iteration (the referenced result) uses only such products, but at step \(k\) it retains only the last vector \(\bA^{k-1}\bv\) and discards the earlier ones.
The Arnoldi process keeps the entire sequence \(\bv,\bA\bv,...,\bA^{k-1}\bv\). We first define the subspace spanned by this sequence and explain why its natural basis is unusable in floating-point arithmetic. We then construct an orthonormal basis one vector at a time and derive the Arnoldi relation. The same relation underlies the Lanczos algorithm in the next section, the GMRES method for linear systems, and the Krylov approximation of the matrix exponential.
The \(k\)th power iterate is a multiple of \(\bA^{k-1}\bv\), so it lies in \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\). Power iteration therefore selects one particular vector from the Krylov subspace, namely the one produced by the polynomial \(p(t)=t^{k-1}\). Any method that searches the whole subspace can do at least as well with the same number of matrix–vector products. the referenced section makes this comparison precise for symmetric matrices.
crumbs: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
NoteDefinition: Krylov Subspace



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) and let \(\bv\in\fR^n\) be nonzero. The \(k\)th Krylov subspace generated by \(\bA\) and \(\bv\) is \[
\begin{align}
\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)=\operatorname{span}\{\bv,\bA\bv,...,\bA^{k-1}\bv\}.
\end{align}
\] Equivalently, \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)=\{p(\bA)\bv : p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\}\), where \(\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\) denotes the polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\).









NoteLemma: Krylov Subspaces Stop Growing at an Invariant Subspace



If \(\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\bA,\bv)=\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\), then \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) is invariant under \(\bA\) in the sense of the referenced result, and \(\mathcal{K}_j(\bA,\bv)=\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) for every \(j\geq k\).








TipProof





Every vector in \(\mathcal{K}_k\) has the form \(p(\bA)\bv\) with \(\deg p\leq k-1\). Multiplying by \(\bA\) gives \(\bA p(\bA)\bv\), which is a polynomial of degree at most \(k\) in \(\bA\) applied to \(\bv\), and therefore lies in \(\mathcal{K}_{k+1}\). Hence \(\bA\mathcal{K}_k\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{k+1}=\mathcal{K}_k\), which is the invariance claim. Since \(\mathcal{K}_{k+2}=\mathcal{K}_{k+1}+\bA\mathcal{K}_{k+1}=\mathcal{K}_k+\bA\mathcal{K}_k=\mathcal{K}_k\), induction gives the second claim.









TipRemark



(Ill-conditioned monomial basis) The vectors \(\bv,\bA\bv,...,\bA^{k-1}\bv\) form a basis of \(\mathcal{K}_k\) whenever the subspace has dimension \(k\), but the basis is useless in practice. By the argument behind power iteration, the normalized vectors \(\bA^j\bv/\|\bA^j\bv\|_2\) converge to the dominant eigenvector, so the later columns of the basis matrix become nearly parallel. Its condition number grows geometrically with \(k\), and rounding errors destroy the information carried by the smaller components.
crumbs: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
16.2 The Arnoldi Process
The remedy is to orthonormalize the Krylov sequence as it is generated. If \(\bv_1,...,\bv_j\) is an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal{K}_j\), we obtain a new direction by multiplying the latest basis vector by \(\bA\) instead of forming \(\bA^j\bv\). We then remove its components along the existing basis by Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization (the referenced result).






NoteDefinition: The Arnoldi Iteration



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) and let \(\bv\in\fR^n\) be nonzero. Set \(\bv_1=\bv/\|\bv\|_2\). For \(j=1,2,...,k\):

Compute \(\bw=\bA\bv_j\).
For \(i=1,...,j\), compute \(h_{ij}=\bv_i^T\bw\) and update \(\bw\leftarrow\bw-h_{ij}\bv_i\).
Compute \(h_{j+1,j}=\|\bw\|_2\).
If \(h_{j+1,j}=0\), stop. Otherwise, set \(\bv_{j+1}=\bw/h_{j+1,j}\).

Step 2 is modified Gram–Schmidt. The coefficients \(h_{ij}\) are collected in the \(k\times k\) upper Hessenberg matrix \(\bH_k\) and in the \((k+1)\times k\) matrix \(\bar{\bH}_k\), which is \(\bH_k\) with the additional row \(h_{k+1,k}\be_k^T\).








NoteTheorem: The Arnoldi Relation



Suppose the Arnoldi iteration completes \(k\) steps with \(h_{j+1,j}\neq0\) for \(j=1,...,k\), and let \(\bV_k=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_k)\). Then:

The columns of \(\bV_k\) are orthonormal and span \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\).
The matrices satisfy $$ \[\begin{align}
\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bH_k+h_{k+1,k}\bv_{k+1}\be_k^T=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k.

\end{align}\] $$
The Hessenberg matrix is the projection of \(\bA\) onto the Krylov subspace, \(\bH_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k\).









TipProof





Step 2 of the iteration subtracts from \(\bw\) its components along \(\bv_1,...,\bv_j\) one at a time. After the subtraction, \(\bw\) is orthogonal to each of these vectors, and normalizing it gives a unit vector \(\bv_{j+1}\) orthogonal to \(\bv_1,...,\bv_j\). Induction on \(j\) proves orthonormality.
Rearranging the definition of \(\bv_{j+1}\) gives the column relation \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bv_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j+1}h_{ij}\bv_i,\qquad j=1,...,k.
\end{align}
\] Placing these \(k\) columns side by side gives \(\bA\bV_k=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\). Separating the last row of \(\bar{\bH}_k\) gives the first form of the referenced equation.
For the span, assume \(\operatorname{span}\{\bv_1,...,\bv_j\}=\mathcal{K}_j\). The column relation expresses \(\bv_{j+1}\) as a combination of \(\bA\bv_j\) and \(\bv_1,...,\bv_j\), and \(\bA\bv_j\in\bA\mathcal{K}_j\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{j+1}\). Hence \(\bv_{j+1}\in\mathcal{K}_{j+1}\). The \(j+1\) orthonormal vectors \(\bv_1,...,\bv_{j+1}\) are linearly independent and lie in \(\mathcal{K}_{j+1}\), whose dimension is at most \(j+1\), so they span it.
Finally, multiplying the referenced equation on the left by \(\bV_k^T\) and using \(\bV_k^T\bV_k=\bI_k\) and \(\bV_k^T\bv_{k+1}=\bzero\) gives \(\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k=\bH_k\).









TipRemark



(Arnoldi cost) Step \(j\) requires one product with \(\bA\) and \(j\) inner products and vector updates of length \(n\). After \(k\) steps the iteration has used \(k\) matrix–vector products and \(O(k^2n)\) additional operations, and it stores \(k+1\) vectors of length \(n\). The orthogonalization cost and storage both grow with \(k\). For a symmetric matrix, the referenced section shows that most of the coefficients \(h_{ij}\) vanish and that the growth disappears.

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
16.3 Ritz Pairs and Breakdown
The matrix \(\bH_k\) is small, so its eigenvalues can be computed by the dense QR algorithm. Its eigenpairs, lifted back to \(\fR^n\) through \(\bV_k\), serve as approximate eigenpairs of \(\bA\). The Arnoldi relation measures their quality without any further products with \(\bA\).






NoteDefinition: Ritz Pairs



Let \(\bH_k\bs=\theta\bs\) with \(\|\bs\|_2=1\). The scalar \(\theta\) is a Ritz value and the unit vector \(\tilde{\bu}=\bV_k\bs\in\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) is the corresponding Ritz vector of \(\bA\) with respect to \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\).








NoteTheorem: Residual of a Ritz Pair



Let \((\theta,\tilde{\bu})\) be a Ritz pair with \(\tilde{\bu}=\bV_k\bs\), and let \(s_k\) denote the last entry of \(\bs\). Then \[
\begin{align}
\bA\tilde{\bu}-\theta\tilde{\bu}=h_{k+1,k}s_k\,\bv_{k+1},
    \qquad
    \|\bA\tilde{\bu}-\theta\tilde{\bu}\|_2=h_{k+1,k}|s_k|.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Multiplying the referenced equation on the right by \(\bs\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\bA\tilde{\bu}
    =\bV_k\bH_k\bs+h_{k+1,k}\bv_{k+1}(\be_k^T\bs)
    =\theta\tilde{\bu}+h_{k+1,k}s_k\bv_{k+1}.
\end{align}
\] Subtracting \(\theta\tilde{\bu}\) and using \(\|\bv_{k+1}\|_2=1\) gives both claims.



The residual norm depends only on \(h_{k+1,k}\) and the last entry of a \(k\)-dimensional eigenvector. We can therefore monitor convergence of every Ritz pair at each step and form \(\tilde{\bu}=\bV_k\bs\) only for the pairs that have converged. A small residual shows that \((\theta,\tilde{\bu})\) is an exact eigenpair of a nearby matrix. For a symmetric matrix, the referenced result then places an eigenvalue within the residual norm of \(\theta\). For a nonnormal diagonalizable matrix, the referenced result multiplies this distance by the condition number of the eigenvector basis, which can be large.






NoteCorollary: Breakdown Gives Exact Eigenvalues



If the Arnoldi iteration stops at step \(k\) because \(h_{k+1,k}=0\), then \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) is invariant under \(\bA\), and every Ritz pair is an exact eigenpair of \(\bA\).








TipProof





When \(h_{k+1,k}=0\), the referenced result gives \(\bA\tilde{\bu}=\theta\tilde{\bu}\) for every Ritz pair. The relation \(\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bH_k\) also shows that \(\bA\) maps the column space of \(\bV_k\), which is \(\mathcal{K}_k\), into itself.

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
text:
17.1 Symmetry Gives a Three-Term Recurrence
When \(\bA\) is real symmetric, the Arnoldi process of the referenced section simplifies in two ways. First, the projected matrix \(\bH_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k\) is symmetric as well as Hessenberg, so it is tridiagonal. Each new basis vector then needs to be orthogonalized only against the two preceding ones, and the cost per step no longer grows with \(k\). Second, the Rayleigh quotient characterization of the referenced result applies to the projected matrix. The characterization shows that the extreme Ritz values are the best estimates of the extreme eigenvalues available from the Krylov subspace.
We first derive the three-term recurrence that defines the Lanczos algorithm (Lanczos 1950). We then show that the extreme Ritz values move monotonically toward the extreme eigenvalues and that they are never worse than the power-iteration estimate obtained with the same number of products. A numerical example compares the two methods. The section ends with the loss of orthogonality that occurs in floating-point arithmetic.
In the Arnoldi iteration, the coefficient \(h_{ij}\) is the component of \(\bA\bv_j\) along \(\bv_i\). the referenced result shows that these components vanish for \(i<j-1\) in exact arithmetic, so the inner loop of Step 2 reduces to two subtractions. The coefficient for \(i=j-1\) is already known from the previous step. Substituting these facts into the referenced result gives the Lanczos iteration.

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
text:
NoteTheorem: Tridiagonal Projection



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and suppose the Arnoldi iteration (the referenced result) completes \(k\) steps. Then \(\bH_k\) is symmetric tridiagonal. Writing \(\alpha_j=h_{jj}\) and \(\beta_j=h_{j+1,j}\), we have \[
\begin{align}
\bH_k=\bT_k=\begin{pmatrix}
        \alpha_1 & \beta_1 & & \\
        \beta_1 & \alpha_2 & \ddots & \\
        & \ddots & \ddots & \beta_{k-1} \\
        & & \beta_{k-1} & \alpha_k
    \end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] and the Arnoldi coefficients satisfy \(h_{ij}=0\) for \(i<j-1\) and \(h_{j-1,j}=\beta_{j-1}\).








TipProof





By the referenced result, \(\bH_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k\). Since \(\bA^T=\bA\), \[
\begin{align}
\bH_k^T=\bV_k^T\bA^T\bV_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k=\bH_k.
\end{align}
\] The matrix \(\bH_k\) is upper Hessenberg, so \(h_{ij}=0\) for \(i>j+1\). Symmetry gives \(h_{ij}=h_{ji}=0\) for \(i<j-1\) as well, which leaves only the diagonal and the two adjacent diagonals. Symmetry also gives \(h_{j-1,j}=h_{j,j-1}=\beta_{j-1}\).










NoteDefinition: The Lanczos Iteration



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and let \(\bv_1\) be a unit vector. Set \(\bv_0=\bzero\) and \(\beta_0=0\). For \(j=1,2,...,k\):

Compute \(\bw=\bA\bv_j-\beta_{j-1}\bv_{j-1}\).
Compute \(\alpha_j=\bv_j^T\bw\) and update \(\bw\leftarrow\bw-\alpha_j\bv_j\).
Compute \(\beta_j=\|\bw\|_2\).
If \(\beta_j=0\), stop. Otherwise, set \(\bv_{j+1}=\bw/\beta_j\).









NoteCorollary: The Lanczos Relation



After \(k\) steps of the Lanczos iteration without breakdown, the matrix \(\bV_k=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_k)\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv_1)\), and \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bT_k+\beta_k\bv_{k+1}\be_k^T,
    \qquad
    \bT_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





In exact arithmetic the Lanczos iteration computes the same vectors and coefficients as the Arnoldi iteration, because it omits only the coefficients that the referenced result shows to be zero. The claims are therefore the referenced result with \(\bH_k=\bT_k\) and \(h_{k+1,k}=\beta_k\).









TipRemark



(Lanczos cost) Each step requires one product with \(\bA\) and \(O(n)\) further operations, independent of \(k\). If only eigenvalues are wanted, the iteration needs to keep just \(\bv_{j-1}\), \(\bv_j\), and the scalars \(\alpha_j,\beta_j\). If Ritz vectors are also wanted, we either store \(\bV_k\) or run the recurrence a second time to form \(\bV_k\bs\).

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
text:
17.2 Ritz Values as Optimal Estimates
The Ritz pairs of the referenced result are now the eigenpairs of the symmetric tridiagonal matrix \(\bT_k\), so the Ritz values are real. the referenced result gives their residuals as \(\beta_k|s_k|\). Symmetry also lets us say how good the Ritz values are. Throughout, let \(\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) and let \(\theta_1^{(k)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_k^{(k)}\) be the eigenvalues of \(\bT_k\).






NoteTheorem: Rayleigh–Ritz Optimality



Let \(R(\bx)=\bx^T\bA\bx/\bx^T\bx\). The extreme Ritz values are the extreme values of the Rayleigh quotient over the Krylov subspace, \[
\begin{align}
\theta_k^{(k)}=\max_{\bx\in\mathcal{K}_k,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R(\bx),
    \qquad
    \theta_1^{(k)}=\min_{\bx\in\mathcal{K}_k,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R(\bx).
\end{align}
\] Consequently, \(\lambda_1\leq\theta_1^{(k)}\) and \(\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\lambda_n\).








TipProof





Every nonzero \(\bx\in\mathcal{K}_k\) has the form \(\bx=\bV_k\by\) with \(\by\in\fR^k\) nonzero. Orthonormality of the columns of \(\bV_k\) gives \(\bx^T\bx=\by^T\by\), and the referenced result gives \(\bx^T\bA\bx=\by^T\bT_k\by\). Hence \[
\begin{align}
R(\bx)=\frac{\by^T\bT_k\by}{\by^T\by}.
\end{align}
\] Applying the referenced result to the symmetric matrix \(\bT_k\) with \(k=1\) and with the largest index shows that the minimum and maximum of this quotient over \(\by\neq\bzero\) are \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) and \(\theta_k^{(k)}\). Applied to \(\bA\), the same characterization shows that \(R(\bx)\) lies in \([\lambda_1,\lambda_n]\) for every nonzero \(\bx\in\fR^n\), which gives the final inequalities.









NoteCorollary: Monotone Convergence of the Extreme Ritz Values



The Ritz values at consecutive steps interlace, \[
\begin{align}
\theta_i^{(k+1)}\leq\theta_i^{(k)}\leq\theta_{i+1}^{(k+1)},
    \qquad i=1,...,k.
\end{align}
\] In particular, \(\theta_k^{(k)}\) increases toward \(\lambda_n\) and \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) decreases toward \(\lambda_1\) as \(k\) grows.








TipProof





The matrix \(\bT_k\) is obtained from \(\bT_{k+1}\) by deleting its last row and column. Applying the referenced result with \(\bT_{k+1}\) in place of \(\bA\) and \(\bT_k\) in place of \(\bB\) gives the interlacing inequalities. Taking \(i=k\) in the right inequality gives \(\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\theta_{k+1}^{(k+1)}\), and taking \(i=1\) in the left inequality gives \(\theta_1^{(k+1)}\leq\theta_1^{(k)}\). the referenced result bounds the two sequences by \(\lambda_n\) and \(\lambda_1\).









NoteCorollary: Lanczos Improves on Power Iteration



Let \(\bA\) be symmetric positive definite, and let \(\lambda^{(k-1)}\) be the Rayleigh quotient estimate of the referenced result after \(k-1\) power steps from \(\bv^{(0)}=\bv_1\). Both \(\lambda^{(k-1)}\) and \(\theta_k^{(k)}\) require \(k\) products with \(\bA\), and \[
\begin{align}
\lambda^{(k-1)}\leq\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\lambda_n.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





The power iterate \(\bv^{(k-1)}\) is a multiple of \(\bA^{k-1}\bv_1\), so it lies in \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv_1)\). Its Rayleigh quotient is \(\lambda^{(k-1)}=R(\bv^{(k-1)})\), which is at most the maximum in the referenced result. Power iteration uses \(k-1\) products to form \(\bv^{(k-1)}\) and one more to evaluate its Rayleigh quotient. Lanczos uses one product per step. Positive definiteness makes \(\lambda_n\) the eigenvalue of largest magnitude, so the two methods approximate the same eigenvalue.



The polynomial form of the referenced result explains the size of the improvement. Every vector in \(\mathcal{K}_k\) is \(p(\bA)\bv_1\) for some \(p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\). Expanding \(\bv_1=\sum_i c_i\bq_i\) in the eigenvectors of \(\bA\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\theta_k^{(k)}=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}}R(p(\bA)\bv_1)
    =\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,p(\lambda_i)^2c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n p(\lambda_i)^2c_i^2}.
\end{align}
\] The quotient is close to \(\lambda_n\) when \(p\) is large at \(\lambda_n\) and small on the rest of the spectrum. Power iteration is restricted to \(p(t)=t^{k-1}\), which separates \(\lambda_n\) from \(\lambda_{n-1}\) only by the factor \((\lambda_{n-1}/\lambda_n)^{k-1}\). Lanczos implicitly selects the best polynomial. A shifted Chebyshev polynomial, which is bounded by one on \([\lambda_1,\lambda_{n-1}]\) and grows rapidly outside it, gives the following bound.






TipRemark



(Kaniel–Paige bound) Let \(\phi\) be the angle between \(\bv_1\) and the eigenvector \(\bq_n\), let \(\gamma=(\lambda_n-\lambda_{n-1})/(\lambda_{n-1}-\lambda_1)\), and let \(T_m(x)=\cosh(m\operatorname{arccosh}x)\) for \(x\geq1\). Then \[
\begin{align}
0\leq\lambda_n-\theta_k^{(k)}\leq(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)\left(\frac{\tan\phi}{T_{k-1}(1+2\gamma)}\right)^2.
\end{align}
\] A proof is given by Golub and Van Loan (Golub and Van Loan 2013). Since \(T_m(1+2\gamma)\) grows roughly like \((1+2\sqrt{\gamma})^m\) when \(\gamma\) is small, the error decreases geometrically at a rate set by the square root of the relative gap. A square root of the same kind appears in the conjugate gradient bound of the referenced result. The analogous bound for \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) follows by applying the result to \(-\bA\). Interior eigenvalues admit weaker bounds and converge more slowly, because no low-degree polynomial can be large at an interior point and small on both sides of it.








NoteExample



(Lanczos and power iteration on a model spectrum) Let \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,...,100)\) and \(\bv_1=(1,...,1)^T/10\). We run Lanczos with full reorthogonalization, so that the computed Ritz values agree with exact arithmetic to rounding level, and compare the error in the largest Ritz value with the error in the power-iteration estimate after the same number of products.
The relative gap is \(\gamma=1/98\), and the power-iteration ratio is \(\lambda_{99}/\lambda_{100}=0.99\). After 40 products the power-iteration estimate has not yet reached one correct digit, whereas the largest Ritz value is correct to about eight significant digits. The bound is valid but conservative at every step. By the symmetry of this spectrum about \(50.5\) and of the starting vector, the error in \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) is the same as the error in \(\theta_k^{(k)}\).
At \(k=40\) the residual of the referenced result for the largest Ritz pair is \(3.7\times10^{-3}\), about four orders of magnitude larger than the eigenvalue error. the referenced result explains the difference. The corollary bounds the distance from the Ritz value to the nearest eigenvalue by the squared residual divided by the distance \(\delta\) from the Ritz value to the other eigenvalues. Here \(\delta\) is about one, and the bound \(1.4\times10^{-5}\) is consistent with the observed error.








TipRemark



(Lanczos and conjugate gradients) The conjugate gradient method of the referenced section builds the same Krylov subspace \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\) for a symmetric positive definite system. Its residuals are multiples of the Lanczos vectors started from \(\bv_1=\br^{(0)}/\|\br^{(0)}\|_2\), and its coefficients determine the entries of \(\bT_k\). the referenced section derives this correspondence and uses it to estimate the extreme eigenvalues during a CG solve.

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
section: 17.3 Loss of Orthogonality and Ghost Eigenvalues
text:
17.3 Loss of Orthogonality and Ghost Eigenvalues
the referenced result relies on the exact orthogonality of \(\bv_{j+1}\) to \(\bv_1,...,\bv_{j-2}\). The Lanczos iteration never enforces this orthogonality explicitly, so rounding errors are free to destroy it.






TipRemark



(Paige’s analysis) In floating-point arithmetic, the computed Lanczos vectors gradually lose mutual orthogonality. Paige showed that the loss is not random (Paige 1976). Let \((\theta_i,\tilde{\bu}_i)\) be a Ritz pair computed from \(\bT_k\), and let \(u\) denote the unit roundoff. Paige’s analysis gives \[
\begin{align}
|\tilde{\bu}_i^T\bv_{k+1}|\approx\frac{u\,\|\bA\|_2}{\beta_k|s_{k,i}|}.
\end{align}
\] The denominator is the residual of the referenced result. The new Lanczos vector therefore acquires a component along \(\tilde{\bu}_i\) precisely as that Ritz pair converges, and orthogonality is lost in the directions of converged Ritz vectors. Once orthogonality to a converged Ritz vector is lost, the iteration begins to approximate the same eigenvalue again and produces repeated copies of it, known as ghost eigenvalues. In the example above, running the iteration without reorthogonalization for \(k=150\) steps gives three Ritz values within \(10^{-6}\) of \(\lambda_{100}=100\) and three within \(10^{-6}\) of \(\lambda_1=1\). At \(k=200\) there are four copies of each.








TipRemark



(Remedies for ghost eigenvalues) Practical implementations use one of three strategies.

Full reorthogonalization. We orthogonalize each new vector against all previous Lanczos vectors. This restores the behavior of exact arithmetic at the Arnoldi cost of \(O(k^2n)\) operations and \(O(kn)\) storage.
Selective reorthogonalization. We orthogonalize only against converged Ritz vectors, and only when Paige’s analysis indicates that orthogonality to them has been lost. The cost is proportional to the number of converged Ritz vectors.
Cullum–Willoughby identification. We run the iteration without reorthogonalization and discard spurious Ritz values afterward by comparing the eigenvalues of \(\bT_k\) with those of the matrix obtained by deleting its first row and column.

text:
17.4 Exercises






WarningExercise

Check. For \(\bT_2\) from the previous exercise, compute both Ritz values and their residuals using the referenced result. Verify the interlacing inequalities of the referenced result between the Ritz value \(\theta_1^{(1)}=\alpha_1\), the two eigenvalues of \(\bT_2\), and the eigenvalues of \(\bA\).
Derive. Using the referenced result, show that \(\theta_{k-1}^{(k)}=\max_{S}\min_{\bx\in S,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R(\bx)\), where \(S\) ranges over two-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathcal{K}_k\). Conclude that \(\theta_{k-1}^{(k)}\leq\lambda_{n-1}\).
Derive. Let \(\bA\) be symmetric positive definite. Show that the power-iteration estimate satisfies \(\lambda_n-\lambda^{(k-1)}\leq(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)\tan^2\phi\,(\lambda_{n-1}/\lambda_n)^{2(k-1)}\), where \(\phi\) is the angle between \(\bv_1\) and \(\bq_n\). Compare the rate with the Kaniel–Paige bound when \(\gamma\) is small.
Compute. Implement the referenced result with an option for full reorthogonalization. Reproduce the table in the example above, and plot all Ritz values against \(k\) for \(k\leq200\) with and without reorthogonalization. Identify the steps at which ghost copies of \(\lambda_{100}\) appear, and relate them to the step at which the largest Ritz value converged.
Explore. Repeat the previous computation with \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,...,99,110)\). Explain, using the polynomial characterization, why the largest Ritz value now converges much faster while the convergence of \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) is essentially unchanged.









NoteFurther reading



Horn and Johnson are a reference for the matrix structure behind the spectral results (Horn and Johnson 2012). The computational treatment in Golub and Van Loan includes symmetric eigensolvers and the SVD (Golub and Van Loan 2013). The original Lanczos and Golub–Kahan papers show how two algorithms in these chapters first appeared (Lanczos 1950; Golub and Kahan 1965).

18.5 Runge’s Phenomenon and Chebyshev Nodes
The error bound contains two decoupled components: \[
\begin{align}
\|f - P_n\|_\infty \leq \frac{\|f^{(n+1)}\|_\infty}{(n+1)!} \|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] The derivative term \(\|f^{(n+1)}\|_\infty\) depends entirely on the analytical smoothness of \(f\), while \(\|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty = \max_{x \in [a, b]} |\prod_{j=0}^n (x - x_j)|\) depends exclusively on the geometric placement of the interpolation nodes.






TipRemark



(Runge phenomenon) Analyticity alone does not make equally spaced interpolation converge. For Runge’s function \(f(x)=1/(1+25x^2)\), the interpolants on equally spaced nodes develop increasing endpoint oscillations and satisfy \[
\begin{align}
\lim_{n \to \infty} \|f - P_n\|_\infty = \infty,
\end{align}
\] even though \(f\) is analytic on the real interval. The growing Lebesgue constant amplifies the approximation error, while the nearby complex poles at \(\pm i/5\) limit the rate of polynomial approximation. The derivative remainder bound above warns that convergence is not automatic, but a divergent upper bound by itself would not prove divergence.


The nodal factor can be made small by placing the nodes well. On \([-1,1]\), the best choice is the set of Chebyshev points \(x_k=\cos\big((2k+1)\pi/(2n+2)\big)\), \(k=0,...,n\), the roots of the Chebyshev polynomial \(T_{n+1}\). For these nodes \(\|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty=2^{-n}\), the smallest value attained by any monic polynomial of degree \(n+1\). the referenced section proves this minimax property and shows that interpolation at Chebyshev points converges geometrically for functions that are analytic in a neighborhood of \([-1,1]\).






TipRemark



The Lebesgue constant \(\Lambda_n = \max_{x \in [a, b]} \sum_{i=0}^n |L_i(x)|\) bounds the stability of polynomial interpolation: \(\|f - P_n\|_\infty \leq (1 + \Lambda_n) \min_{Q \in \mathcal{P}_n} \|f - Q\|_\infty\).

For equally spaced nodes, \(\Lambda_n \sim O\left(\frac{2^n}{n \log n}\right)\) grows exponentially.
For Chebyshev nodes, \(\Lambda_n \sim \frac{2}{\pi} \log(n+1) + O(1)\) grows only logarithmically, remaining near-optimal.

title: 19  Chebyshev Polynomials and Minimax Approximation
text:
19.1 Two Failures of Polynomial Interpolation
Chebyshev polynomials provide an orthogonal polynomial basis on \([-1,1]\) and a principled choice of nodes for high-degree interpolation. Under the coordinate mapping \(x=\cos\theta\), algebraic polynomials become cosine series. The scaled polynomial \(2^{1-n}T_n(x)\) uniquely minimizes the uniform norm among monic polynomials of degree \(n\). Chebyshev nodes replace the exponential growth of the uniform-grid Lebesgue constant by logarithmic growth, and analytic functions then admit geometrically convergent approximations.
Approximating a continuous function \(f \in C([-1, 1])\) by polynomial interpolation encounters two distinct failure modes. The first is algebraic. Vandermonde systems in the monomial basis are often ill-conditioned, so a coefficient calculation may lose accuracy even when the interpolating polynomial is well defined. The second is analytical. For functions such as Runge’s example, interpolation at equally spaced nodes diverges near the endpoints even in exact arithmetic. These are different failures and require different remedies.
For the analytical failure, the referenced result gives the remedy. With \(n\) nodes \(x_1,...,x_n\) and the monic nodal polynomial \(\omega_n(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n(x-x_j)\), the theorem bounds the interpolation error by \[
\begin{align}
\|f-p_{n-1}\|_\infty\leq\frac{\|f^{(n)}\|_\infty}{n!}\,\|\omega_n\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] The first factor depends only on \(f\), and the second only on the nodes. Choosing the nodes to minimize \(\|\omega_n\|_\infty\) is therefore a minimax problem over monic polynomials of degree \(n\), which this section solves.

section: 19.3 Roots, Extrema, and the Nodal Error Polynomial
text:
19.3 Roots, Extrema, and the Nodal Error Polynomial






NoteTheorem: Zeros and Extreme Points of \(T_n\)



For each \(n \geq 1\), the polynomial \(T_n(x)\) has:

Exactly \(n\) distinct real zeros in \((-1, 1)\), given by \[
\begin{align}
x_j = \cos\left( \frac{2j - 1}{2n} \pi \right), \qquad j = 1, ..., n.
\end{align}
\]
Exactly \(n+1\) alternating extreme points on \([-1, 1]\), given by \[
\begin{align}
y_j = \cos\left( \frac{j\pi}{n} \right), \qquad j = 0, ..., n,
\end{align}
\] at which \(T_n(y_j) = (-1)^j\).









TipProof





The condition \(T_n(x) = 0\) corresponds to \(\cos(n\theta) = 0\) for \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\). The cosine function vanishes when \(n\theta = (j - 1/2)\pi = \frac{2j-1}{2}\pi\) for integers \(j\). Restricting \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) restricts \(j \in \{1, ..., n\}\). Setting \(x_j = \cos\theta_j\) gives the \(n\) distinct roots.
Similarly, \(T_n(x)\) attains its extreme values \(\pm 1\) when \(|\cos(n\theta)| = 1\), which requires \(n\theta = j\pi\) for \(j \in \{0, ..., n\}\). At these points, \(T_n(y_j) = \cos(j\pi) = (-1)^j\).









NoteDefinition: Chebyshev Nodes



The Chebyshev interpolation nodes of degree \(n\) are the \(n\) roots of \(T_n(x)\): \[
\begin{align}
x_j = \cos\left( \frac{2j - 1}{2n} \pi \right), \qquad j = 1, ..., n.
\end{align}
\] These nodes cluster quadratically near the interval endpoints \(\pm 1\), with local separation \(x_{j+1} - x_j \sim O(1/n^2)\) near the boundaries and \(O(1/n)\) in the interior.








NoteTheorem: Representation of the Chebyshev Nodal Polynomial



Let \(\{x_j\}_{j=1}^n\) be the Chebyshev nodes from the referenced result. The monic nodal polynomial satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\omega_n(x) = \prod_{j=1}^n (x - x_j) = 2^{1-n} T_n(x).
\end{align}
\] Consequently, the uniform norm of the nodal polynomial is \[
\begin{align}
\|\omega_n\|_\infty = 2^{1-n} \|T_n\|_\infty = 2^{1-n}.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Both \(\omega_n(x)\) and \(T_n(x)\) are polynomials of degree \(n\) sharing the same \(n\) distinct roots \(x_1, ..., x_n\). Therefore, they are proportional: \(T_n(x) = C \omega_n(x)\) for some nonzero constant \(C\). By the referenced result, the leading coefficient of \(T_n(x)\) is \(2^{n-1}\), whereas \(\omega_n(x)\) is monic with leading coefficient \(1\). Hence \(C = 2^{n-1}\), which gives \(\omega_n(x) = 2^{1-n} T_n(x)\).
Because \(T_n(\cos\theta) = \cos(n\theta)\), \(|T_n(x)| \leq 1\) for all \(x \in [-1, 1]\), and this maximum is attained at \(x = 1\). Thus \(\|T_n\|_\infty = 1\), which confirms that \(\|\omega_n\|_\infty = 2^{1-n}\).

19.6 Exercises






WarningExercise




Derive. (Clenshaw’s evaluation algorithm) Evaluating a Chebyshev sum \(p(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k T_k(x)\) by explicitly forming \(T_k(x)\) is inefficient and prone to floating-point error. Clenshaw’s recurrence evaluates the sum in \(O(n)\) flops without computing trigonometric functions.

Define the backward sequence \(b_{n+2} = b_{n+1} = 0\), and for \(k = n, n-1, ..., 1\), \[
\begin{align}
b_k = 2x b_{k+1} - b_{k+2} + c_k.
\end{align}
\] Show that \(p(x) = c_0 + x b_1 - b_2\).
Prove that this backward recurrence is algebraically equivalent to evaluating \(p(x)\) by substituting the three-term relation \(T_{k+1} = 2x T_k - T_{k-1}\).
Implement Clenshaw’s algorithm in Python and compare its runtime against explicit monomial expansion for \(n = 50\).

Check. (Equioscillation on a concrete polynomial) Let \(m(x)=2^{1-4}T_4(x)\).

Expand \(m\) in the monomial basis and verify that it is monic.
Evaluate \(m\) at \(y_j=\cos(j\pi/4)\) for \(j=0,...,4\) and verify the alternating values \(\pm1/8\).
Choose any monic quartic \(q\neq m\), evaluate it on a fine grid, and confirm numerically that \(\|q\|_\infty>1/8\), as predicted by the referenced result.

Compute. (Lebesgue constant computation and Runge comparison) The Lebesgue function is \(\lambda_n(x) = \sum_{j=1}^n |\ell_j(x)|\), where \(\ell_j(x)\) are the Lagrange cardinal polynomials.

Write a script to evaluate \(\lambda_n(x)\) on a fine grid of \(10^4\) points in \([-1, 1]\) for uniform nodes and Chebyshev nodes for \(n \in \{5, 10, 15, 20\}\).
Plot the maximum \(\Lambda_n = \max_{x \in [-1, 1]} \lambda_n(x)\) versus \(n\) on a semilog scale. Verify that \(\Lambda_n\) grows exponentially for uniform nodes and logarithmically for Chebyshev nodes.
Interpolate Runge’s function \(f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2)\) with \(n = 20\) using both node sets. Explain the boundary behavior in terms of the Bernstein ellipse parameter \(\rho\).

Derive. (Chebyshev differentiation matrix) Let \(\bx = (x_0, x_1, ..., x_n)^T\) be the Chebyshev extreme nodes \(x_j = \cos(j\pi/n)\).

Derive the entries of the spectral differentiation matrix \(\bD_n \in \fR^{(n+1) \times (n+1)}\) that maps the nodal values \(\mathbf{f} = (f(x_0), ..., f(x_n))^T\) to the exact derivative values of the polynomial interpolant \(\mathbf{f}' = \bD_n \mathbf{f}\).
Show that the diagonal entries satisfy \(D_{00} = \frac{2n^2 + 1}{6}\) and \(D_{nn} = -\frac{2n^2 + 1}{6}\).
Verify that the row sums of \(\bD_n\) vanish identically: \(\bD_n \mathbf{1} = \bzero\).

Explore. (Bernstein ellipse parameter for Runge’s function) Consider \(f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + 25x^2}\) on \([-1, 1]\).

Find the complex poles of \(f(z)\) in \(\fC\).
Determine the largest value of \(\rho\) such that the Bernstein ellipse \(\mathcal{E}_\rho\) does not contain either pole.
Using the referenced result, compute the asymptotic error decay factor \(\rho^{-1}\) and predict how many Chebyshev modes are needed to achieve machine precision \(\|f - p_n\|_\infty \leq 10^{-16}\).

title: 20  Numerical Quadrature
text:
20.1 Degree of Exactness and Interpolatory Quadrature
Numerical quadrature approximates the definite integral of a continuous function \(f : [a, b] \to \fR\) by a finite linear combination of sampled function values: \[
\begin{align}
I(f) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx Q_n(f) = \sum_{i=0}^n w_i f(x_i).
\end{align}
\] The points \(x_i \in [a, b]\) are the quadrature nodes, and the scalar coefficients \(w_i \in \fR\) are the quadrature weights. The design of quadrature rules balances algebraic precision, computational cost, and numerical stability.
The standard criterion for evaluating a quadrature rule is its algebraic precision, defined by the highest degree of polynomials it integrates without error.

title: 21  Fourier Analysis as Change of Basis
text:
21.1 The Discrete Fourier Transform
Fourier analysis provides the mathematical framework for decomposing functions, discrete signals, and linear operators into frequency components. In scientific computing, the Fourier transform diagonalizes shift-invariant operators, accelerates convolution from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(n \log n)\) operations, and yields spectral differentiation methods with exponential convergence for smooth periodic solutions.
(Running example: Poisson matrix) On a periodic grid, Fourier modes diagonalize the discrete Laplacian. With Dirichlet boundary conditions, sine modes play the same role for the Poisson matrix of the referenced section. Their eigenvalues determine the conditioning of that matrix and the smoothing behavior used by multigrid in the referenced section.
We consider discrete signals defined on a uniform periodic grid of \(n\) points. The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) expands a vector in the orthonormal basis of discrete complex exponentials.

title: 21  Fourier Analysis as Change of Basis
text:
21.4 Spectral Differentiation
For smooth periodic functions, differentiation in the Fourier domain replaces finite-difference stencils with exact multiplication in frequency.






NoteTheorem: Spectral Differentiation of Periodic Functions



Let \(u: \fR \to \fC\) be a \(2\pi\)-periodic function with continuous derivatives through order \(m\). Representing \(u\) by its Fourier series \(u(x) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty \hat{u}_k e^{ikx}\), the derivative has Fourier coefficients \[
\begin{align}
\widehat{(u')}_k = ik \hat{u}_k.
\end{align}
\] If \(u\) is analytic in a strip \(\{z \in \fC : |\operatorname{Im}(z)| < d\}\), the truncation error of the discrete spectral derivative converges geometrically to zero: \[
\begin{align}
\max_{x_j} |u'(x_j) - (D_n \bu)_j| = O(e^{-d n/2}).
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Differentiating the series term by term gives \(\frac{d}{dx} \sum_{k} \hat{u}_k e^{ikx} = \sum_{k} (ik \hat{u}_k) e^{ikx}\), which proves the coefficient formula. If \(u\) is analytic in the strip of half-width \(d\), shifting the contour of integration in \(\hat{u}_k = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} u(x) e^{-ikx} dx\) to \(x - i \operatorname{sign}(k) d\) yields the bound \(|\hat{u}_k| \leq M e^{-d |k|}\). The aliased grid modes satisfy \(|k| \geq n/2\). Summing the tail of the neglected high-frequency modes gives \(\sum_{|k| \geq n/2} |k| |\hat{u}_k| \leq 2M \sum_{k=n/2}^\infty k e^{-d k} = O(e^{-d n/2})\).

Write the indices \(0, 1, ..., 7\) in 3-bit binary notation (\(b_2 b_1 b_0\)).
Reverse the bits (\(b_0 b_1 b_2\)) to construct the bit-reversal permutation vector \(\mathbf{p}\).

Apply the spectral derivative to \(u(x) = \sin(x)\) and measure the maximum pointwise error against \(\cos(x)\). Confirm that error reaches machine precision for small \(n\).
Apply the spectral derivative to \(v(x) = \frac{1}{2 + \cos(x)}\). Estimate the decay constant \(d\) from the referenced result and confirm geometric convergence.
Explain why applying Fourier differentiation to a non-periodic function such as \(w(x) = x\) causes Gibbs oscillations and algebraic error decay \(O(1/n)\).

title: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation
text:
22.1 Differential Operators and Discretization
(Running example: Poisson matrix) The matrix constructed here is the model sparse system for the rest of this part. The following sections solve it by stationary iteration, conjugate gradients, and multigrid, and each method uses a different property of the same matrix. Its eigenvectors are discrete sine modes (the referenced result), and its eigenvalues explain the convergence rate of each method.
Differential equations become matrix problems after discretization. The finite matrix should preserve the main structure of the operator: sparsity, symmetry, definiteness, spectrum, and conditioning.

title: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation
text:
NoteDefinition: Linear Operator



Map \(\mathcal{A}: X \to Y\) between function spaces satisfying: \[
\begin{align}
\mathcal{A}(\alpha u + v) = \alpha \mathcal{A}u + \mathcal{A}v.
\end{align}
\] Matrices are finite-dimensional operators, whereas \(\frac{d}{dx}\) and \(\nabla^2\) are infinite-dimensional.








NoteDefinition: Dirichlet Poisson Problem



The one-dimensional Poisson problem with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary data is \[
\begin{align}
-u''(x)=f(x),\qquad 0<x<1,\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0.
\end{align}
\] The boundary conditions are part of the problem data.








NoteDefinition: Grid Function



For \(n\) interior grid points, let \(h=1/(n+1)\) and \(x_i=ih\), \(i=1,...,n\). A grid function is the vector \[
\begin{align}
\bu=(u_1,...,u_n)^T,\qquad u_i\approx u(x_i).
\end{align}
\] The boundary values are fixed separately by the boundary conditions.








NoteDefinition: Finite Difference Stencil



Approximating \(u''(x)\) on a grid with spacing \(h\): \[
\begin{align}
u''(x_k) \approx \frac{u(x_{k-1}) - 2u(x_k) + u(x_{k+1})}{h^2}.
\end{align}
\] Accuracy: Second-order \(O(h^2)\) via Taylor expansion.








WarningExercise



Derive.

Taylor expand \(u(x+h)\) and \(u(x-h)\) about \(x\).
Add the two expansions.
Solve for \(u''(x)\).
Identify the leading error term and prove the \(O(h^2)\) claim in the referenced result.









NoteDefinition: 1-D Discrete Laplacian



Discretizing \(-d^2/dx^2\) on \([0,1]\) with \(u(0)=u(1)=0\) yields the tridiagonal system \(\bT \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{f}\): \[
\begin{align}
\bT = \frac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1) \in \fR^{n \times n}.
\end{align}
\]








TipRemark



(Sparsity) Each row of \(\bT\) uses only the grid point and its two neighbors. This locality is why finite difference matrices are sparse.








NoteTheorem: Spectrum Convergence



Eigenvalues of \(\bT\) are \(\lambda_k = \frac{4}{h^2} \sin^2(\frac{k\pi}{2(n+1)})\). As \(n \to \infty\), \(\lambda_k \to k^2 \pi^2\) (eigenvalues of continuous \(-d^2/dx^2\)).








WarningExercise



Derive.

Let \((\bv_k)_j=\sin(jk\pi h)\) with \(h=1/(n+1)\).
Compute the \(j\)-th entry of \(\bT\bv_k\).
Use \(\sin(A-B)+\sin(A+B)=2\sin A\cos B\).
Use \(1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)\).
Derive the eigenvalue formula in the referenced result.
Let \(h\to 0\) with fixed \(k\) and recover \(k^2\pi^2\).









NoteTheorem: Discrete Poisson Structure



The matrix \(\bT\) in the referenced result is sparse, symmetric positive definite, and has condition number \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bT)=O(h^{-2}).
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Sparsity and symmetry follow directly from the tridiagonal stencil \(\bT = \frac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1)\). For any grid vector \(\bu \in \fR^n\) with boundary conditions \(u_0 = u_{n+1} = 0\), the quadratic form expands as a sum of squared forward differences: \[
\begin{align}
\bu^T \bT \bu
    &= \frac{1}{h^2} \sum_{i=1}^n u_i (2u_i - u_{i-1} - u_{i+1}) \\
    &= \frac{1}{h^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (u_i^2 - u_i u_{i-1} + u_i^2 - u_i u_{i+1}) \\
    &= \frac{1}{h^2} \sum_{i=0}^n (u_{i+1} - u_i)^2.
\end{align}
\] Because \(u_0 = 0\), if \(\bu^T\bT\bu = 0\), then \(u_{i+1} - u_i = 0\) for all \(i\), forcing \(u_1 = ... = u_n = 0\). Hence \(\bu^T\bT\bu > 0\) for all \(\bu \neq \bzero\), proving that \(\bT\) is SPD.
By the referenced result, the extremal eigenvalues are \[
\begin{align}
\lambda_{\min} &= \lambda_1 = \frac{4}{h^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{h^2}\left(\frac{\pi h}{2} + O(h^3)\right)^2 = \pi^2 + O(h^2), \\
    \lambda_{\max} &= \lambda_n = \frac{4}{h^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{n\pi h}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{h^2}\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{h^2}(1 - O(h^2)).
\end{align}
\] The 2-norm condition number is therefore \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bT) = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} = \frac{4/h^2 + O(1)}{\pi^2 + O(h^2)} = \frac{4}{\pi^2 h^2} + O(1) = O(h^{-2}).
\end{align}
\]









WarningExercise



Derive.

Use the stencil to count the number of nonzeros in \(\bT\).
Use the quadratic form \(\bu^T\bT\bu\) to show positive definiteness for nonzero interior grid functions.
Use the referenced result to estimate \(\lambda_{\min}\) and \(\lambda_{\max}\).
Derive the condition number estimate in the referenced result.

title: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation
text:
22.2 Operator Norms and Conditioning






NoteDefinition: Boundedness



An operator is bounded if \(\|\mathcal{A}u\|_Y \leq C \|u\|_X\) for some \(C < \infty\).

Matrices are always bounded.
Differential operators are unbounded.









TipRemark



(Ill-Conditioning from Unboundedness) Because the continuous Laplacian is unbounded, its discretization \(\bT\) becomes increasingly ill-conditioned as \(h \to 0\): \[
\begin{align}
\kappa(\bT) = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} \approx \frac{4/h^2}{\pi^2} = O(h^{-2}).
\end{align}
\] Refining the grid \(2\times\) quadruples the condition number.








TipRemark



(Solver consequence) Dense Gaussian elimination ignores sparsity. For Poisson matrices, sparse Cholesky, CG with preconditioning, multigrid, or FFT-based solvers are the natural algorithms, depending on geometry and boundary conditions.

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
text:
23.1 Matrix Splittings and Stationary Iterations
Direct methods such as Gaussian elimination and Cholesky factorization compute exact solutions up to machine roundoff in a finite number of arithmetic operations. However, for the large-scale linear systems arising from the discretization of three-dimensional partial differential equations or network models, direct factorizations become computationally prohibitive. the referenced section showed that the Cholesky factor of a three-dimensional Poisson matrix has \(O(n^{4/3})\) nonzero entries and costs \(O(n^2)\) flops even with a nested dissection ordering, so the factor can exceed the available memory long before the matrix does.
Iterative methods avoid this storage cost. Instead of transforming the matrix through elimination, an iterative solver generates a sequence of approximations \(\bx^{(0)}, \bx^{(1)}, \bx^{(2)}, ...\) to the solution \(\bx^* = \bA^{-1}\bb\). The central computational primitive is the matrix–vector product \(\bv \mapsto \bA\bv\). For a stored sparse matrix this product requires \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA))\) operations and storage, whereas for a matrix-free operator it may require only a small number of work vectors. Whether the complete method scales well also depends on convergence and preconditioning.
(Running example: Poisson matrix) Return to the tridiagonal Poisson matrix of the referenced section. The matrix is sparse enough for cheap matrix–vector products, but its condition number grows as the mesh is refined. One example therefore separates methods that use only sparsity from methods that also use symmetry, definiteness, or multiple grid scales.
The classical approach to designing an iterative solver is matrix splitting. We decompose the coefficient matrix \(\bA\) into the difference of two matrices, \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \bM - \mathbf{N},
\end{align}
\] where the splitting matrix \(\bM\) is nonsingular and easily invertible. The linear system \(\bA\bx = \bb\) is then algebraically equivalent to \(\bM\bx = \mathbf{N}\bx + \bb\).

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
text:
NoteDefinition: Stationary Iteration



Given a splitting \(\bA = \bM - \mathbf{N}\), the corresponding stationary iteration computes successive approximations via the fixed-point recurrence \[
\begin{align}
\bM\bx^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{N}\bx^{(k)} + \bb \iff \bx^{(k+1)} = \bT\bx^{(k)} + \bc,
\end{align}
\] where \(\bT = \bM^{-1}\mathbf{N} = \bI - \bM^{-1}\bA\) is the iteration matrix and \(\bc = \bM^{-1}\bb\) is the modified right-hand side vector.








TipRemark



(Fixed-point interpretation) A stationary iteration is a linear fixed-point mapping. The exact solution \(\bx^*\) satisfies \(\bx^* = \bT\bx^* + \bc\). The effectiveness of the method depends entirely on the choice of \(\bM\): the matrix \(\bM\) should be as close to \(\bA\) as possible to minimize the magnitude of \(\bT\), while remaining computationally cheap to invert at each step.

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
text:
23.3 Krylov Subspaces and Matrix-Free Solvers
A stationary method applies the same splitting at every step. A Krylov method instead chooses the iterate \(\bx^{(k)}\) from the affine space \(\bx^{(0)}+\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\), where \(\mathcal{K}_k\) is the Krylov subspace of the referenced result generated by the initial residual. The basis for this space is built by the Arnoldi process of the referenced section, or by the Lanczos recurrence when \(\bA\) is symmetric. The conjugate gradient and GMRES methods differ in the optimality criterion used to select \(\bx^{(k)}\).






NoteTheorem: Krylov Polynomial Representation



Let \(\bx^{(0)}\) be an initial guess with residual \(\br^{(0)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(0)}\). Any iterate \(\bx^{(k)}\) belonging to the affine Krylov space \(\bx^{(0)} + \mathcal{K}_k(\bA, \br^{(0)})\) can be represented as \[
\begin{align}
\bx^{(k)} = \bx^{(0)} + p_{k-1}(\bA)\br^{(0)},
\end{align}
\] where \(p_{k-1}\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k-1\). The corresponding residual vector satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\br^{(k)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(k)} = q_k(\bA)\br^{(0)},
\end{align}
\] where \(q_k(t) = 1 - t p_{k-1}(t)\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k\) satisfying the normalization constraint \(q_k(0) = 1\).








TipRemark



(Matrix-free computation) Krylov subspace methods never require explicit access to the individual entries of \(\bA\). They interact with the linear operator exclusively by computing matrix–vector products \(\bv \mapsto \bA\bv\). Consequently, linear systems can be solved efficiently even when the matrix is defined implicitly as a differential operator or a numerical simulation routine.








NoteDefinition: Stopping Criteria for Iterative Solvers



Because the true error \(\be^{(k)} = \bx^{(k)} - \bx^*\) is unobservable, termination is determined using the computable residual vector \(\br^{(k)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(k)}\). Common stopping criteria include:

Relative residual test: \(\frac{\|\br^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\bb\|_2} \leq `tol`\).
Preconditioned relative residual test: \(\frac{\|\bM^{-1}\br^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\bM^{-1}\bb\|_2} \leq `tol`\).
Step difference test: \(\frac{\|\bx^{(k+1)} - \bx^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\bx^{(k+1)}\|_2} \leq `tol`\).









WarningExercise




Compute. Consider the matrix \(\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and the splitting \(\bM = 4\bI\). Compute the iteration matrix \(\bT = \bI - \bM^{-1}\bA\), find its eigenvalues, and evaluate its spectral radius \(\rho(\bT)\).
Check. For the splitting above, determine the number of iterations required to reduce the initial error by a factor of \(10^{-6}\).
Derive. Prove that if \(\|\bT\| < 1\) for some induced matrix norm, then the error satisfies \(\|\be^{(k)}\| \leq \frac{\|\bT\|}{1 - \|\bT\|} \|\bx^{(k)} - \bx^{(k-1)}\|\).
Derive. Let \(\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\) and let \(\br^{(0)} \in \fR^n\). the referenced result shows that \(\dim\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\) stops growing once the Krylov subspace is invariant. Prove the complementary statement: before that step, the dimension increases by exactly one at each step.

title: 24  Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, and SOR Methods
text:
24.1 The Jacobi Method
The classical stationary iterations represent the earliest systematic approaches to solving linear systems iteratively. They partition the matrix \(\bA\) into its diagonal, strictly lower triangular, and strictly upper triangular components: \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \bD - \bL_A - \bU_A,
\end{align}
\] where \(\bD = \operatorname{diag}(a_{11}, ..., a_{nn})\), \(-\bL_A\) is the strictly lower triangular part of \(\bA\), and \(-\bU_A\) is the strictly upper triangular part of \(\bA\). By choosing different combinations of these components for the splitting matrix \(\bM\), we obtain the Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel, and Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR) algorithms.
The Jacobi method assumes that the diagonal elements dominate the matrix. It computes the \((k+1)\)-th estimate of each unknown \(x_i\) exclusively from the \(k\)-th estimates of all other variables.

title: 24  Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, and SOR Methods
text:
24.4 Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR)
The Successive Over-Relaxation method accelerates the convergence of Gauss–Seidel by taking a weighted linear combination of the previous iterate and the new Gauss–Seidel update.






NoteDefinition: Successive Over-Relaxation Scheme



Let \(\omega > 0\) be a relaxation parameter. The SOR method computes the updated components via \[
\begin{align}
x_i^{(k+1)} = (1 - \omega) x_i^{(k)} + \frac{\omega}{a_{ii}} \left( b_i - \sum_{j < i} a_{ij} x_j^{(k+1)} - \sum_{j > i} a_{ij} x_j^{(k)} \right).
\end{align}
\] In matrix notation, this corresponds to the splitting \(\bM_\omega = \frac{1}{\omega}\bD - \bL_A\) and \(\mathbf{N}_\omega = \left( \frac{1}{\omega} - 1 \right)\bD + \bU_A\). The iteration matrix is \[
\begin{align}
\bT_\omega = (\bD - \omega \bL_A)^{-1} \left( (1 - \omega)\bD + \omega \bU_A \right).
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Ostrowski–Reich Theorem and the Optimal Parameter



If \(\bA\) is symmetric positive definite, then the SOR iteration converges if and only if the relaxation parameter satisfies \[
\begin{align}
0 < \omega < 2.
\end{align}
\] Furthermore, if \(\bA\) is consistently ordered (such as the standard tridiagonal or block-tridiagonal Poisson discretization matrices) and the Jacobi spectral radius is \(\rho(\bT_J) < 1\), then the optimal relaxation parameter that minimizes \(\rho(\bT_\omega)\) is \[
\begin{align}
\omega^* = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho(\bT_J)^2}}.
\end{align}
\] With this optimal choice, the spectral radius satisfies \(\rho(\bT_{\omega^*}) = \omega^* - 1\).








TipRemark



(Acceleration for discrete Poisson equations) For the 1D discrete Laplacian on a grid with spacing \(h\), the Jacobi spectral radius is \(\rho(\bT_J) = \cos(\pi h) \approx 1 - \frac{1}{2}\pi^2 h^2\). Consequently, Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel require \(O(h^{-2}) = O(n^2)\) iterations to converge. With optimal SOR, \(\omega^* \approx 2 - 2\pi h\), yielding \(\rho(\bT_{\omega^*}) \approx 1 - 2\pi h\). This reduces the required iteration count to \(O(h^{-1}) = O(n)\), providing an order-of-magnitude computational speedup.








WarningExercise




Compute. Compute the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iteration matrices for \(\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\). Find their spectral radii and verify that \(\rho(\bT_{GS}) = \rho(\bT_J)^2\).
Explore. Let \(\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Show that \(\bA\) is symmetric but indefinite, and prove that both Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel diverge.
Derive. Prove the Kahan theorem: for any matrix \(\bA\) with nonzero diagonal entries, \(\rho(\bT_\omega) \geq |\omega - 1|\), which implies that SOR can only converge if \(0 < \omega < 2\).
Compute. Write a Python script to solve the 1D discrete Poisson equation with \(n=50\) grid points using Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, and optimal SOR. Plot the residual norm versus iteration number on a semilogarithmic scale.

title: 25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
text:
25.1 Quadratic Optimization and Steepest Descent
The Conjugate Gradient (CG) method of Hestenes and Stiefel is a standard iterative solver for large, sparse, symmetric positive definite systems. Unlike a stationary iteration determined by one fixed splitting, CG selects the approximation \(\bx^{(k)}\) that minimizes the error in the \(\bA\)-norm over the affine Krylov subspace \(\bx^{(0)}+\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\).
Symmetry and conjugacy reduce this expanding-subspace minimization to a short recurrence. The resulting algorithm stores only a few vectors of length \(n\) and uses one matrix–vector product per iteration.
(Running example: Poisson matrix) The discrete Poisson matrix is SPD, so CG applies without changing the model. Its slowly varying eigenmodes explain why the unpreconditioned iteration deteriorates under refinement and why the coarse-grid ideas of the referenced section are relevant.
The mathematical foundation of the Conjugate Gradient method lies in the equivalence between solving an SPD linear system and minimizing a convex quadratic energy functional.

title: 25  The Conjugate Gradient Method

25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
text:
25.4 Convergence Rate and Preconditioning
Although CG terminates in \(n\) steps in exact arithmetic, its primary utility in scientific computing is as a rapid iterative solver for which \(k \ll n\).






NoteTheorem: Chebyshev Error Bound for Conjugate Gradient



Let \(\bA\) be symmetric positive definite with 2-norm condition number \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\). The error at step \(k\) satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\|\bx^{(k)} - \bx^*\|_\bA}{\|\bx^{(0)} - \bx^*\|_\bA} \leq 2 \left( \frac{\sqrt{\kappa} - 1}{\sqrt{\kappa} + 1} \right)^k.
\end{align}
\]








NoteCorollary: Termination with Distinct Eigenvalues



If \(\bA\) has only \(m\) distinct eigenvalues, CG reaches the exact solution in at most \(m\) iterations in exact arithmetic.








TipProof





Let the distinct eigenvalues be \(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_m\). The polynomial \[
\begin{align}
p_m(t)=\prod_{j=1}^m\left(1-\frac{t}{\lambda_j}\right)
\end{align}
\] has degree \(m\), satisfies \(p_m(0)=1\), and vanishes on the spectrum of \(\bA\). The spectral theorem therefore gives \(p_m(\bA)=\bzero\). CG minimizes the energy-norm error over all vectors whose error has the form \(p(\bA)\be^{(0)}\) with \(p(0)=1\). Since \(p_m(\bA)\be^{(0)}=\bzero\) is available after \(m\) steps, the minimum error is zero.









TipRemark



(The square root condition number advantage) The convergence bound for the Conjugate Gradient method depends on \(\sqrt{\kappa}\), whereas stationary iterations depend directly on \(\kappa\). For an ill-conditioned system with \(\kappa = 10^4\), the reduction factor per iteration for stationary methods is approximately \((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1) \approx 0.9998\), whereas for CG it is \((\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1) = 99/101 \approx 0.9802\), converging fifty times faster per step.








TipRemark



(Superlinear convergence) The Chebyshev bound is a worst-case guarantee for an arbitrary spectrum. When the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) are grouped into tight clusters with only a few isolated outliers, CG eliminates the outlying eigenmodes in the first few iterations and then converges at a rate governed by the clustered eigenvalues. This behavior is termed superlinear convergence.








NoteDefinition: Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG)



Let \(\bM\) be a symmetric positive definite preconditioner. The Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient algorithm solves \(\bA\bx = \bb\) by transforming the geometry using the inner product induced by \(\bM^{-1}\). At each step, a linear system \(\bM\bz^{(k)} = \br^{(k)}\) is solved, and the step lengths and direction updates become \[
\begin{align}
\alpha_k = \frac{\br^{(k)T}\bz^{(k)}}{\bp^{(k)T}\bA\bp^{(k)}}, \qquad \beta_k = \frac{\br^{(k+1)T}\bz^{(k+1)}}{\br^{(k)T}\bz^{(k)}}.
\end{align}
\] A well-chosen preconditioner clusters the eigenvalues of \(\bM^{-1}\bA\) near \(1\), ensuring rapid convergence in few iterations.








WarningExercise




Check. For a diagonal SPD matrix with three distinct eigenvalues, construct the polynomial in the referenced result and verify that it annihilates the matrix.
Derive. Derive the formula for \(\alpha_k\) by explicitly minimizing the single-variable quadratic function \(g(\alpha) = \phi(\bx^{(k)} + \alpha \bp^{(k)})\) with respect to \(\alpha\).
Compute. Implement the Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient algorithm in Python using an incomplete Cholesky preconditioner, and test it on a 2D discrete Laplacian of size \(100 \times 100\).

title: 26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method
text:
26.1 Reduction to Hessenberg Least Squares
When a linear system \(\bA\bx = \bb\) is nonsymmetric or indefinite, the quadratic energy minimization framework of the Conjugate Gradient method ceases to apply. The Faber–Manteuffel theorem characterizes the exceptional matrix classes that admit an optimal Krylov method with a fixed short recurrence. No such recurrence gives optimal residuals for arbitrary nonsymmetric matrices, so GMRES retains the full Arnoldi basis.
The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) method of Saad and Schultz chooses, at every step \(k\), a vector \(\bx^{(k)}\) in the affine Krylov subspace \(\bx^{(0)} + \mathcal{K}_k(\bA, \br^{(0)})\) that minimizes the Euclidean residual norm \(\|\bb - \bA\bx\|_2\) (Saad and Schultz 1986). GMRES constructs an orthonormal basis for the growing Krylov subspace by the Arnoldi process of the referenced section (Arnoldi 1951) and reduces the original problem to a small upper-Hessenberg least-squares problem. The minimizing residual is unique, and the iterate is unique when the reduced least-squares problem has full column rank.
Let \(\br^{(0)}=\bb-\bA\bx^{(0)}\) be nonzero and let \(\beta=\|\br^{(0)}\|_2\). We run the Arnoldi iteration of the referenced result from \(\bv_1=\br^{(0)}/\beta\). By the referenced result, after \(k\) steps the columns of \(\bV_k\) form an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\) and \(\bA\bV_k=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\). These two facts reduce the residual minimization in \(\fR^n\) to a small least-squares problem.
