title: 26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method
text:
26.2 Solution via Givens Rotations






NoteTheorem: Incremental QR Factorization of the Hessenberg Matrix



At step \(k\), applying the previously accumulated Givens rotations \(\bG_1, ..., \bG_{k-1}\) transforms the first \(k-1\) entries of the new column of \(\bar{\bH}_k\). The subdiagonal entry at position \((k+1, k)\) is then eliminated using a new Givens rotation \(\bG_k\) defined by \[
\begin{align}
\bG_k = \begin{pmatrix} c_k & s_k \\ -s_k & c_k \end{pmatrix}, \qquad c_k = \frac{h_{kk}^{(k-1)}}{\sqrt{(h_{kk}^{(k-1)})^2 + h_{k+1,k}^2}}, \quad s_k = \frac{h_{k+1,k}}{\sqrt{(h_{kk}^{(k-1)})^2 + h_{k+1,k}^2}}.
\end{align}
\] Applying \(\bG_k ... \bG_1\) transforms \(\bar{\bH}_k\) into an upper triangular matrix \(\bR_k\) with a zero final row, and transforms the right-hand side vector \(\beta \be_1\) into \(\bg_{k+1} = (\gamma_1, ..., \gamma_k, \gamma_{k+1})^T\). The residual norm at iteration \(k\) is obtained without forming \(\bx^{(k)}\): \[
\begin{align}
\|\br^{(k)}\|_2 = |\gamma_{k+1}|.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(\bQ_k = \bG_k ... \bG_1 \in \fR^{(k+1) \times (k+1)}\) denote the product of Givens rotations. Because each Givens rotation is an orthogonal transformation on \(\fR^{k+1}\), \(\bQ_k\) is orthogonal. The least-squares problem satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\min_{\by \in \fR^k} \|\beta \be_1 - \bar{\bH}_k \by\|_2^2
    =
    \min_{\by \in \fR^k} \|\bQ_k(\beta \be_1 - \bar{\bH}_k \by)\|_2^2
    =
    \min_{\by \in \fR^k} \left\| \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_{1:k} \\ \gamma_{k+1} \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} \bR_k \\ \bzero^T \end{pmatrix} \by \right\|_2^2.
\end{align}
\] Expanding the squared Euclidean norm: \[
\begin{align}
\min_{\by \in \fR^k} \left( \|\gamma_{1:k} - \bR_k \by\|_2^2 + |\gamma_{k+1}|^2 \right).
\end{align}
\] Because \(\bR_k \in \fR^{k \times k}\) is upper triangular and nonsingular (assuming no earlier breakdown), we can choose \(\by_k = \bR_k^{-1} \gamma_{1:k}\) to make the first term identically zero. The remaining squared residual is exactly \(|\gamma_{k+1}|^2\), proving that \(\|\br^{(k)}\|_2 = |\gamma_{k+1}|\).









TipRemark



(Happy breakdown vs. stagnation) If the subdiagonal entry \(h_{k+1,k}\) vanishes, the referenced result shows that the Krylov subspace is invariant under \(\bA\). When \(\bA\) is nonsingular, its restriction to this invariant subspace is nonsingular, so the GMRES least-squares problem has residual zero and \(\bx^{(k)}\) is the exact solution. Termination for this reason is called happy breakdown. Stagnation is a different phenomenon. The Krylov space may continue to grow while its image under \(\bA\) contributes no useful correction to the residual. Non-normality, an unfavorable polynomial approximation problem, or a poor preconditioner can all cause this behavior, and the residual history alone does not identify which one is responsible.

title: 26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method
text:
26.3 Restarted GMRES and Practical Considerations






NoteDefinition: Restarted GMRES(\(m\))



Full GMRES requires storing \(k\) basis vectors of length \(n\), incurring \(O(kn)\) memory storage and \(O(k^2 n)\) orthogonalization flops. To avoid memory exhaustion on large systems, the algorithm is restarted every \(m\) steps:

Run \(m\) steps of GMRES starting from \(\bx^{(0)}\) to produce \(\bx^{(m)}\).
Compute the residual \(\br^{(m)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(m)}\).
Clear the Krylov basis vectors, set \(\bx^{(0)} \leftarrow \bx^{(m)}\), and repeat.









TipRemark



(The trade-off of restarting) Restarted GMRES(\(m\)) bounds memory usage to \(O(mn)\) and bounds orthogonalization cost per cycle. However, restarting discards the accumulated Krylov subspace and destroys the global optimality property. If \(m\) is chosen too small, the algorithm may stagnate completely.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
27.1 Oscillating Error and the Smoothing Property
(Running example: Poisson matrix) We again use the Poisson matrix, now together with the hierarchy of grids from which it arose. Stationary iteration exposed the slow modes, whereas multigrid succeeds by changing the scale on which those modes are represented.
Classical stationary iterations such as Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel converge slowly because the smooth (low-frequency) error components decay slowly. High-frequency, oscillatory components decay within a few sweeps. A Fourier analysis of the error makes this asymmetry precise, and multigrid is built on it. The smoother removes the oscillatory error components, and the remaining smooth error is passed to a coarser grid, where it becomes oscillatory and cheap to resolve.
Frequency-Dependent Error Decay in Jacobi Iteration For the 1D model problem, the Jacobi update reads \[
\begin{align}
x_i^{(k+1)} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(x_{i-1}^{(k)} + x_{i+1}^{(k)}\bigr) + \tfrac{1}{2}b_i.
\end{align}
\] Each new value is the average of its two neighbors plus a source term. Consider two extreme error profiles at some iteration:
Jacobi acts as a local averaging filter that pulls each value toward the mean of its neighbors. Oscillations cancel in that average, whereas smooth trends do not. Starting from a random initial guess, the error spans all frequencies. After a handful of sweeps the oscillatory components are gone, but the smooth residual remains, requiring a coarser grid for resolution.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
Oscillatory error: neighboring values often have opposite signs, so averaging damps many high-frequency modes rapidly. The exact alternating mode is an exception for unweighted Jacobi: its sign flips without shrinking. Weighted Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel supplies the smoothing used in multigrid.
Smooth error (\(e_i \propto \sin(j\pi h)\) for small \(j\), slowly varying): neighbors of node \(i\) carry nearly the same value as \(e_i\) itself, so their average barely moves things. The error barely changes per sweep.








TipRemark



(Choosing a solver) The structure of the coefficient matrix determines the method. The following summary collects the recommendations of the preceding sections.

Dense symmetric positive definite. Cholesky factorization (the referenced result), with \(n^3/3\) flops and no pivoting.
Large sparse symmetric positive definite. Preconditioned conjugate gradients (the referenced section) or multigrid, with \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA))\) work per iteration.
Dense general square. Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting (the referenced result), with \(2n^3/3\) flops and the backward error of the referenced result.
Large sparse general square. Preconditioned GMRES (the referenced section).
Overdetermined with full column rank. Householder QR (the referenced result), which avoids the squared condition number of the normal equations.
Rank-deficient or nearly rank-deficient. The SVD (the referenced result), which determines the numerical rank and the minimum-norm solution.









WarningExercise



Explore. (Observing oscillating error) Set \(n = 63\), \(\bb = \bzero\), and \(\bx^* = \bzero\), so the error equals the iterate exactly. Run Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel from the same random initial vector \(\bx^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \bI)\).

Plot the error profile \(\be^{(k)} = \bx^{(k)}\) at iterations \(k = 0, 1, 3, 10, 20\). Describe how the spectral composition of the error changes. Observe the behavior of the high-frequency components.
Decompose \(\be^{(k)}\) into Fourier mode amplitudes \(\hat{e}_j^{(k)} = \langle \be^{(k)}, \phi^{(j)}\rangle / \|\phi^{(j)}\|^2\) and plot \(|\hat{e}_j^{(k)}|\) vs. \(j\) at the same iterations. Which modes decay fast, which persist?
The Jacobi iteration matrix has eigenvalues \(\mu_j = \cos(j\pi h)\). Use this to predict the amplitude of mode \(j\) after \(k\) sweeps as a function of the initial amplitude \(|\hat{e}_j^{(0)}|\). Does your plot match the prediction?
After 20 sweeps, what does the remaining error look like? Argue, using the eigenvalue formula, why no fine-grid iteration alone can efficiently eliminate it, necessitating a coarse-grid correction.









NoteDefinition: Fourier Modes on a Uniform Grid



Consider the 1D model problem with the \(n \times n\) tridiagonal matrix \(\bA\) having \(2\) on the main diagonal and \(-1\) on the off-diagonals (the finite-difference discretization of \(-u'' = f\) on \([0,1]\) scaled by \(h^2\)). Let \(h = 1/(n+1)\). The Fourier modes are the vectors \[
\begin{align}
\phi^{(k)}_j = \sin(kj\pi h), \quad j = 1,...,n, \quad k = 1,...,n.
\end{align}
\] These form an orthogonal basis for \(\fR^n\) (by discrete sine orthogonality) and diagonalize \(\bA\): \[
\begin{align}
\bA\phi^{(k)} = \lambda_k\,\phi^{(k)}, \qquad \lambda_k = 2 - 2\cos(k\pi h) = 4\sin^2\!\Bigl(\frac{k\pi h}{2}\Bigr).
\end{align}
\] Small \(k\) yields long-wavelength (smooth) modes, while large \(k\) yields short-wavelength (oscillatory) modes.








NoteTheorem: Eigenvalues of the Jacobi Iteration Matrix



For the 1D model problem, the Jacobi iteration matrix \(\bT_J = \bI - \tfrac{1}{2}\bA\) has eigenvalues \[
\begin{align}
\mu_k = \cos(k\pi h), \quad k = 1, ..., n,
\end{align}
\] with eigenvectors \(\phi^{(k)}\). After \(\nu\) Jacobi sweeps, mode \(k\) of the error is scaled by \(\mu_k^\nu = \cos^\nu(k\pi h)\).








TipProof





Since \(\bD = 2\bI\), the Jacobi iteration matrix is \(\bT_J = \bI - \frac{1}{2}\bA\). Applying \(\bT_J\) to the eigenvector \(\phi^{(k)}\): \[
\begin{align}
\bT_J\phi^{(k)}
  &= \left(\bI - \frac{1}{2}\bA\right)\phi^{(k)}
  = \phi^{(k)} - \frac{1}{2}\bA\phi^{(k)} \\
  &= \phi^{(k)} - \frac{1}{2}\lambda_k\phi^{(k)}
  = \left(1 - \frac{\lambda_k}{2}\right)\phi^{(k)}.
\end{align}
\] Substituting \(\lambda_k = 2 - 2\cos(k\pi h)\) yields \[
\begin{align}
1 - \frac{\lambda_k}{2}
  = 1 - (1 - \cos(k\pi h))
  = \cos(k\pi h).
\end{align}
\] Therefore \(\bT_J\phi^{(k)} = \cos(k\pi h)\phi^{(k)}\).









NoteDefinition: Low- and High-Frequency Modes



With respect to a grid of mesh size \(h = 1/(n+1)\), partition the \(n\) Fourier modes by frequency:

Low-frequency (smooth) modes: \(k = 1, ..., \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\), where \(k\pi h \in (0, \pi/2)\). These satisfy \(\mu_k = \cos(k\pi h) \in (0,1)\), and for small \(k\), \(\mu_k \approx 1 - (k\pi h)^2/2 \approx 1\), so these modes decay slowly.
High-frequency (oscillatory) modes: \(k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1, ..., n\), where \(k\pi h \in (\pi/2, \pi)\).









TipRemark



Standard Jacobi (\(\omega = 1\)) is a poor smoother, because the highest-frequency mode (\(k = n\)) satisfies \(\mu_n = \cos(n\pi h) = \cos(\pi n/(n+1)) \approx -1\), so the iterate oscillates in sign rather than decaying. Weighted (damped) Jacobi with \(\omega = 2/3\) fixes this by controlling the entire high-frequency band.








NoteDefinition: Weighted Jacobi Iteration



The weighted Jacobi method introduces a damping parameter \(\omega \in (0,1)\): \[
\begin{align}
\bx^{(k+1)} = \bx^{(k)} + \omega\bD^{-1}\bigl(\bb - \bA\bx^{(k)}\bigr),
\end{align}
\] with iteration matrix \(\bT_\omega = \bI - \omega\bD^{-1}\bA\) and eigenvalues \[
\begin{align}
\mu_k(\omega) = 1 - \omega(1 - \cos(k\pi h)).
\end{align}
\] The standard multigrid choice is \(\omega = 2/3\).








NoteTheorem: Smoothing Property of Weighted Jacobi



For the 1D model problem with \(\omega = 2/3\), the smoothing factor \[
\begin{align}
\bar{\mu} = \max_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor < k \leq n}\,|\mu_k(2/3)| = \frac{1}{3}.
\end{align}
\] That is, every high-frequency component of the error is reduced by at least \(2/3\) in a single weighted Jacobi step.








TipProof





For \(k > n/2\), we have \(k\pi h \in (\pi/2, \pi)\), so \(1 - \cos(k\pi h) \in (1, 2)\). With \(\omega = 2/3\): \[
\begin{align}
\mu_k(2/3) = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(k\pi h)) \in \Bigl(1 - \tfrac{4}{3},\; 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}\Bigr) = \Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{3},\; \tfrac{1}{3}\Bigr).
\end{align}
\] Hence \(|\mu_k| < 1/3\) for all high-frequency modes. The supremum \(1/3\) is approached as \(k \to \lfloor n/2\rfloor^+\) (where \(\cos(k\pi h) \to 0^-\)).









TipRemark



After \(\nu\) weighted Jacobi sweeps, every high-frequency error component is reduced by \((1/3)^\nu\). The remaining error is dominated by smooth modes, which are nearly constant on the scale of \(h\). This smooth, slowly-varying error is the target of the coarse-grid correction in multigrid.








NoteExample



Eigenvalue spectrum of \(\bT_{2/3}\) for \(n = 15\), \(h = 1/16\).
The eigenvalues \(\mu_k = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(k\pi/16))\) for selected \(k\):

\(k = 1\) (smoothest): \(\mu_1 \approx 0.981\) (minimal decay per sweep).
\(k = 4\): \(\mu_4 = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(\pi/4)) \approx 0.804\) (slow decay).
\(k = 8\): \(\mu_8 = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(\pi/2)) = 1/3 \approx 0.333\).
\(k = 12\): \(\mu_{12} = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(3\pi/4)) \approx -0.138\) (rapid decay).
\(k = 15\) (most oscillatory): \(\mu_{15} \approx -0.330\) (magnitude bounded by \(1/3\)).

Modes \(k \geq 8\) all satisfy \(|\mu_k| \leq 1/3\), confirming the smoothing property. Modes \(k \leq 7\) range from \(0.63\) to \(0.98\) and are essentially untouched by the smoother.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
27.2 The Two-Grid Correction Scheme
A smooth error on a fine grid of mesh size \(h\) looks oscillatory on a coarser grid of mesh size \(2h\). More precisely, the smooth fine-grid modes (\(k < n/2\)) oscillate at wavelength \(> 2h\) and are well-represented on the coarse grid. Once the high-frequency components have been attenuated by the smoother, the remaining error lives in a low-dimensional smooth subspace that a direct solve on a coarse grid of size \(n/2\) can eliminate efficiently.






NoteDefinition: Prolongation Operator



The prolongation (or interpolation) operator \(\bP: \fR^{m} \to \fR^{n}\) (where \(m = (n-1)/2\) for grids satisfying \(n = 2m+1\)) transfers a coarse-grid vector to the fine grid by linear interpolation. For a coarse-grid vector \(\bv \in \fR^m\), the fine-grid vector \(\bP\bv \in \fR^n\) is defined by \[
\begin{align}
(\bP\bv)_{2j} = v_j, \qquad (\bP\bv)_{2j-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(v_{j-1} + v_j), \quad j = 1, ..., m,
\end{align}
\] with boundary conventions \(v_0 = v_{m+1} = 0\). In matrix form, \(\bP\) is \(n \times m\) with entries \(1\) at coarse-grid points and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) weights at fine-grid midpoints.








NoteDefinition: Restriction Operator



The restriction operator \(\bR: \fR^{n} \to \fR^{m}\) transfers a fine-grid vector to the coarse grid. The standard full-weighting restriction averages each coarse point with its fine-grid neighbors: \[
\begin{align}
(\bR\bw)_j = \tfrac{1}{4}w_{2j-1} + \tfrac{1}{2}w_{2j} + \tfrac{1}{4}w_{2j+1}, \quad j = 1, ..., m.
\end{align}
\] In matrix form, \(\bR = \tfrac{1}{2}\bP^T\). This choice ensures that the Galerkin coarse-grid operator \(\bA_c = \bR\bA\bP\) is SPD whenever \(\bA\) is SPD.








TipRemark



The relationship \(\bR = \tfrac{1}{2}\bP^T\) is called the variational principle and guarantees that \(\bA_c = \bR\bA\bP\) is a consistent, spectrally equivalent discretization on the coarse grid. For the 1D model problem, \(\bA_c\) equals the natural finite-difference matrix on the \(2h\)-grid exactly. This special property simplifies analysis but does not hold in general for variable-coefficient or higher-dimensional problems.








NoteDefinition: Two-Grid Correction Scheme



Given \(\bA\bx = \bb\) on the fine grid, one step of the two-grid (TG) method from an iterate \(\bx^{(0)}\) is:

Pre-smoothing: Apply \(\nu_1 \geq 0\) smoother steps to get \(\tilde{\bx}\).
Residual: Compute \(\br = \bb - \bA\tilde{\bx}\).
Restrict: Form the coarse residual \(\br_c = \bR\br \in \fR^m\).
Coarse solve: Solve \(\bA_c\be_c = \br_c\) exactly for \(\be_c \in \fR^m\).
Prolong and correct: Set \(\hat{\bx} = \tilde{\bx} + \bP\be_c\).
Post-smoothing: Apply \(\nu_2 \geq 0\) smoother steps to \(\hat{\bx}\) to get \(\bx^{(1)}\).

The coarse-grid system \(\bA_c\be_c = \br_c\) solves the residual equation: if \(\bx^* - \tilde{\bx}\) is smooth and lies in the range of \(\bP\), this recovers the error exactly.








NoteTheorem: Ideal Coarse-Grid Correction



If the error \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bx^* - \tilde{\bx}\) lies in the range of \(\bP\) (i.e., \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bP\boldsymbol{\delta}\) for some \(\boldsymbol{\delta} \in \fR^m\)), then the two-grid correction recovers the exact solution: \(\hat{\bx} = \bx^*\).








TipProof





Let \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bx^* - \tilde{\bx} = \bP\boldsymbol{\delta}\) for some \(\boldsymbol{\delta} \in \fR^m\). The residual vector is \[
\begin{align}
\br = \bb - \bA\tilde{\bx} = \bA(\bx^* - \tilde{\bx}) = \bA\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bA\bP\boldsymbol{\delta}.
\end{align}
\] Applying the restriction operator \(\bR\): \[
\begin{align}
\br_c = \bR\br = \bR\bA\bP\boldsymbol{\delta} = \bA_c\boldsymbol{\delta}.
\end{align}
\] Since \(\bA_c\) is nonsingular, solving the coarse problem \(\bA_c\be_c = \br_c\) yields \[
\begin{align}
\be_c = \bA_c^{-1}\br_c = \bA_c^{-1}\bA_c\boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{\delta}.
\end{align}
\] Prolongating the coarse correction and updating gives \[
\begin{align}
\hat{\bx} = \tilde{\bx} + \bP\be_c = \tilde{\bx} + \bP\boldsymbol{\delta} = \tilde{\bx} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bx^*.
\end{align}
\] Thus the coarse-grid correction eliminates the error exactly.









NoteExample



Two-grid correction on the 1D model problem (\(n = 7\), \(h = 1/8\)).
Take \(\bA\) the \(7 \times 7\) tridiagonal matrix with \(2/-1\), \(\bb = \mathbf{1}\), \(\bx^{(0)} = \bzero\). After \(\nu_1 = 2\) weighted Jacobi sweeps the residual norm is \(\|\br\| \approx 0.82\), and after 20 Jacobi sweeps it is \(\approx 0.32\). By contrast, a single two-grid step with \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 = 2\) reduces the residual to \(\approx 0.08\), which is roughly a \(10\times\) improvement over pure smoothing at equal cost, because the coarse-grid solve resolves the smooth error components that the smoother leaves behind.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
27.3 The Multigrid V-Cycle
The two-grid method replaces the fine-grid iteration matrix with one that damps all error components, at the cost of an exact coarse-grid solve. For large problems the coarse grid may itself be large. Multigrid applies the idea recursively. Instead of solving the coarse-grid problem exactly, it applies the two-grid scheme again at the coarser level, and so on, until the coarsest grid is trivially small (a single unknown). This gives the V-cycle.






NoteDefinition: Multigrid Grid Hierarchy



For \(n = 2^L - 1\), define \(L\) nested grids with mesh sizes \(h_\ell = 2^{-\ell}\), giving \(n_\ell = 2^\ell - 1\) interior points at level \(\ell = 1, ..., L\). The finest grid is \(\ell = L\) (mesh size \(h\)) and the coarsest is \(\ell = 1\) (a single point). At each level \(\ell\) we have a system matrix \(\bA_\ell\) (built via Galerkin: \(\bA_{\ell-1} = \bR_\ell\bA_\ell\bP_\ell\)), restriction \(\bR_\ell: \fR^{n_\ell} \to \fR^{n_{\ell-1}}\), and prolongation \(\bP_\ell: \fR^{n_{\ell-1}} \to \fR^{n_\ell}\).








NoteDefinition: Multigrid V-Cycle



\(\mathtt{MG}(\ell,\, \bx,\, \bb)\): one multigrid V-cycle at level \(\ell\), returning an improved approximation to \(\bA_\ell\bx = \bb\):

Base case (\(\ell = 1\)): return \(\bA_1^{-1}\bb\) (exact solve on a \(1 \times 1\) system).
Pre-smoothing: \(\bx \leftarrow S_\ell^{\nu_1}(\bx,\,\bb)\) (\(\nu_1\) steps of the smoother at level \(\ell\)).
Restrict residual: \(\br_{\ell-1} \leftarrow \bR_\ell(\bb - \bA_\ell\bx)\).
Coarse-grid correction: \(\be_{\ell-1} \leftarrow \mathtt{MG}(\ell-1,\,\bzero,\,\br_{\ell-1})\).
Correct: \(\bx \leftarrow \bx + \bP_\ell\be_{\ell-1}\).
Post-smoothing: \(\bx \leftarrow S_\ell^{\nu_2}(\bx,\,\bb)\) (\(\nu_2\) steps of the smoother).
Return \(\bx\).

Calling \(\mathtt{MG}\) once as the coarse-grid solver in step 4 gives the V-cycle. Calling it twice gives the W-cycle, which is more robust on difficult problems at higher cost.








TipRemark



A single V-cycle descends from the finest level \(L\) to the coarsest level \(1\) (the down stroke'') applying pre-smoothing and restriction, then ascends back (theup stroke’’) applying prolongation and post-smoothing. Typical choices are \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 = 1\) or \(2\). The W-cycle replaces the single recursive call in step 4 with two calls, more aggressively correcting smooth error at the cost of roughly \(\log n\) extra work.








NoteTheorem: Mesh-Independent Convergence Principle



Consider a family of SPD discretizations with grid-independent smoothing and approximation constants. If the chosen smoother damps the components not represented on the coarse grid and the transfer operators approximate the remaining smooth components uniformly in \(h\), then the two-grid error-propagation operator satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\|\be^{(k+1)}\|_{\bA} \leq \rho\,\|\be^{(k)}\|_{\bA},
\end{align}
\] where \(\rho<1\) is independent of the mesh size. The same conclusion extends to a V-cycle when the recursive coarse solve preserves these uniform estimates. For the uniform-grid Poisson problem, weighted Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel with standard interpolation and restriction satisfies these hypotheses.








TipProof





The complete proof depends on the discretization and transfer operators. Its structure combines two estimates:

Smoothing property: After \(\nu\) smoother steps, the high-frequency components of the error satisfy \(\|\bT_\omega^\nu\be\|_{\bA} \leq \eta(\nu)\|\be\|_{\bA}\) where \(\eta(\nu) \to 0\) as \(\nu \to \infty\), uniformly in \(h\).
Approximation property: The coarse-grid correction resolves the smooth components: \(\|(I - \bP\bA_c^{-1}\bR\bA)\be\|_{\bA} \leq C h^2 \|\bA\be\|\) for a constant \(C\) independent of \(h\).

The smoother first removes error that cannot be represented accurately on the coarse grid. The coarse-grid correction then approximates the remaining component. Uniform constants in these two estimates give a contraction factor independent of \(h\). This argument is a proof outline. A numerical value of \(\rho\) requires the precise smoother, boundary conditions, and transfer operators.









TipRemark



For classical iterations on the 1D Poisson problem, \(\rho(\bT_J) = \cos(\pi h) \approx 1 - \pi^2h^2/2 \to 1\) as \(h \to 0\), requiring \(O(h^{-2}) = O(n)\) Jacobi iterations. With the V-cycle, the number of iterations to reach a fixed tolerance is bounded by a constant independent of \(n\). The cost per V-cycle is \(O(n)\) (geometric series over levels), making the total cost \(O(n)\), which is the optimal asymptotic complexity for this class of problems.








NoteTheorem: \(O(n)\) Complexity of the V-Cycle



For \(L\)-level multigrid on a problem with \(n = n_L\) unknowns at the finest level, each V-cycle requires \(O(n)\) floating-point operations, independent of the number of levels \(L\).








TipProof





Let \(W_\ell\) denote the work at level \(\ell\) per V-cycle. At each level, the smoother and residual computation cost \(O(n_\ell)\), and \(n_\ell = n_{L}/2^{L-\ell}\). The total work is \[
\begin{align}
W = \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} O(n_\ell) = O\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} \frac{n}{2^{L-\ell}}\right) = O(n)\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\frac{1}{2^j} < O(2n) = O(n).
\end{align}
\] The geometric series converges regardless of \(L\), giving \(O(n)\) total.









NoteExample



Multigrid vs. classical iterations on the 2D Poisson problem.
Discretize \(-\Delta u = f\) on the unit square with an \(n \times n\) grid (\(h = 1/(n+1)\)), giving \(N = n^2\) unknowns. Approximate iteration counts to reduce the residual by \(10^{-8}\), and total work in units of \(N\) multiplications:
For \(n = 100\) (\(N = 10^4\)): multigrid requires \(\approx 10\) V-cycles while Gauss-Seidel requires \(\approx 4000\) iterations. At \(n = 1000\) (\(N = 10^6\)): multigrid still requires \(\approx 10\) V-cycles, demonstrating mesh-independence, while Gauss-Seidel requires \(\approx 400{,}000\) iterations.








WarningExercise



Compute. (Smoothing property) For the \(n = 15\) 1D model problem:

Compute the eigenvalues \(\mu_k\) of the standard Jacobi (\(\omega = 1\)) and weighted Jacobi (\(\omega = 2/3\)) iteration matrices. Plot \(|\mu_k|\) as a function of \(k\) on a single figure.
Starting from a random initial error \(\be^{(0)} \in \fR^{15}\), apply 3 steps of each method. Plot the initial and final errors, and describe qualitatively how each method reshapes the error.
Identify the ``worst-case’’ mode (largest \(|\mu_k|\)) for each method over the high-frequency range \(k > 7\). Why is the standard Jacobi smoother inadequate for multigrid?









WarningExercise



Compute. (Two-grid implementation) Implement the two-grid correction scheme for the 1D model problem with \(n = 2^m - 1\) interior points.

Write restrict(r) using the full-weighting formula and prolongate(e) using linear interpolation for transferring between a fine grid and the next coarser grid.
Implement two\_grid(A, b, x0, nu1, nu2) with \(\nu_1\) pre-smoothing and \(\nu_2\) post-smoothing steps of weighted Jacobi (\(\omega = 2/3\)) and an exact coarse-grid solve via np.linalg.solve.
For \(m = 6\) (\(n = 63\)), plot residual norm versus iteration count for: (a) weighted Jacobi alone, (b) repeated two-grid cycling. Use a semi-log scale. Estimate the per-cycle convergence factor \(\rho\) for the two-grid method.









WarningExercise



Compute. (Multigrid V-cycle) Extend the two-grid implementation to a full V-cycle.

Implement vcycle(x, b, A\_list, level, nu1, nu2) recursively. At level 1 (a single unknown), solve exactly. Test first on the two-grid case to verify it matches your Part 2 implementation.
Run the V-cycle on the 1D Poisson problem with \(n = 2^{10} - 1 = 1023\) and \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 = 1\). Measure the empirical convergence factor \(\rho_k = \|\br^{(k)}\| / \|\br^{(k-1)}\|\) for \(k = 1, ..., 15\). Is it approximately constant (mesh-independent)?
Repeat for \(n = 2^{12} - 1 = 4095\). Compare the convergence factors. Then vary \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) and report the convergence factor versus the extra cost per cycle.









NoteFurther reading



Saad and Greenbaum give complementary treatments of Krylov methods and preconditioning (Saad 2003; Greenbaum 1997). The original conjugate-gradient and GMRES papers remain readable (Hestenes and Stiefel 1952; Saad and Schultz 1986). For multigrid, the tutorial by Briggs, Henson, and McCormick is a natural next step (Briggs et al. 2000).

title: 28  Randomized Methods in Linear Algebra
text:
28.1 Trace and Diagonal Estimation
Some quantities are expensive to compute exactly but inexpensive to estimate. The diagonal of \(\bA^{-1}\) requires \(n\) solves, a truncated SVD of an \(m\times n\) matrix costs \(O(mn\min(m,n))\) flops, and the Cholesky factor of a sparse matrix may be much denser than the matrix. Randomized methods replace each exact calculation by one that acts on a few random vectors or random samples. They accept an error that is controlled in expectation or with high probability, and they reuse one expensive object, such as a factorization or a product with \(\bA\), for every sample.
We first estimate traces and diagonals from random probe vectors. We then compute low-rank approximations from the range of \(\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) for a random matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\). Finally, we show how random sampling limits fill during Gaussian elimination on graph Laplacians, which produces a preconditioner for the conjugate gradient method.
The trace of \(\bA^{-1}\) and the diagonal of \(\bA^{-1}\) appear as sums of variances in statistics, as effective resistances in graphs, and as sensitivities of linear models. Computing \(\operatorname{diag}(\bA^{-1})\) exactly requires solving \(\bA\bx=\be_i\) for every \(i\). The estimators below use only products \(\bz\mapsto\bA\bz\), or solves with \(\bA\), applied to a few random vectors \(\bz\).
Averaging \(k\) independent samples divides the variance by \(k\). For a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, \(\|\bA\|_F^2=\sum_i\lambda_i^2\leq(\sum_i\lambda_i)^2=\operatorname{tr}(\bA)^2\), so with Gaussian probes the relative standard deviation of the averaged estimate is at most \(\sqrt{2/k}\). The error decreases like \(k^{-1/2}\), independently of \(n\), which is the usual Monte Carlo rate. One hundred probes therefore give a relative standard deviation of at most about fourteen percent, and the estimator is most useful when this accuracy is sufficient or when \(\|\bA\|_F\) is much smaller than \(\operatorname{tr}(\bA)\) (Hutchinson 1990).
To estimate \(\operatorname{diag}(\bA^{-1})\), we replace \(\bA\bz_l\) by \(\bA^{-1}\bz_l\) (Bekas et al. 2007). One sparse factorization of \(\bA\) is computed once, and each probe then costs one pair of triangular solves. For \(k\ll n\), this replaces \(n\) solves by \(k\) solves. Bekas, Kokiopoulou, and Saad also use structured probe vectors that are orthogonal on blocks of the matrix, which removes the error from entries within those blocks.

title: 28  Randomized Methods in Linear Algebra
text:
NoteTheorem: Hutchinson’s Trace Estimator



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(\bz\in\fR^n\) have independent entries with mean zero and variance one. Then \(\mathbb{E}[\bz^T\bA\bz]=\operatorname{tr}(\bA)\). If the entries of \(\bz\) are \(\pm1\) with equal probability, then \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}(\bz^T\bA\bz)=2\Big(\|\bA\|_F^2-\sum_{i=1}^na_{ii}^2\Big).
\end{align}
\] If the entries of \(\bz\) are standard normal, then \(\operatorname{Var}(\bz^T\bA\bz)=2\|\bA\|_F^2\).








TipProof





Expanding the quadratic form gives \(\bz^T\bA\bz=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}z_iz_j\). Since \(\mathbb{E}[z_iz_j]\) is one for \(i=j\) and zero otherwise, the expectation is \(\sum_ia_{ii}\).
For \(\pm1\) entries, \(z_i^2=1\), so \(\bz^T\bA\bz-\operatorname{tr}(\bA)=2\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}z_iz_j\) by symmetry. The products \(z_iz_j\) with \(i<j\) have mean zero and variance one, and two different products are uncorrelated because \(\mathbb{E}[z_iz_jz_kz_l]=0\) unless \(\{i,j\}=\{k,l\}\). Hence the variance is \(4\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}^2=2\sum_{i\neq j}a_{ij}^2\).
For standard normal entries, write \(\bA=\bQ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bQ^T\) by the referenced result. The vector \(\bg=\bQ^T\bz\) is again standard normal, and \(\bz^T\bA\bz=\sum_i\lambda_ig_i^2\). Each \(g_i^2\) has variance two and the \(g_i\) are independent, so the variance is \(2\sum_i\lambda_i^2=2\|\bA\|_F^2\).










NoteProposition: Diagonal Estimator



Let \(\bz_1,...,\bz_k\) be independent vectors with independent \(\pm1\) entries, and let \(\odot\) denote the entrywise product. Then \[
\begin{align}
\bd_k=\frac1k\sum_{l=1}^k\bz_l\odot(\bA\bz_l)
\end{align}
\] satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\bd_k]=\operatorname{diag}(\bA)\).








TipProof





Entry \(i\) of \(\bz\odot(\bA\bz)\) is \(z_i\sum_ja_{ij}z_j=a_{ii}+\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ij}z_iz_j\), because \(z_i^2=1\). The second sum has mean zero, so each term of the average has mean \(a_{ii}\).

title: 28  Randomized Methods in Linear Algebra
text:
28.2 Randomized Low-Rank Approximation
By the referenced result, the best rank-\(k\) approximation of \(\bA\) is given by its truncated SVD. Computing the full SVD of a large matrix in order to keep a few singular triplets wastes almost all of the work. If the singular values decay, the dominant left singular vectors span most of the range of \(\bA\). A product \(\bA\boldsymbol{\omega}\) with a random vector \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is a random combination of the columns of \(\bA\), and it lies mostly in that dominant subspace. A few such products therefore span most of the dominant range.






NoteDefinition: Randomized SVD



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\), let \(k\) be the target rank, and let \(p\geq2\) be an oversampling parameter.

Draw \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\in\fR^{n\times(k+p)}\) with independent standard normal entries.
Form \(\bY=\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) and compute its thin QR factorization \(\bY=\bQ\bR\).
Form \(\bB=\bQ^T\bA\in\fR^{(k+p)\times n}\) and compute its SVD \(\bB=\tilde{\bU}\bsigma\bV^T\).
Return the approximate SVD \(\bA\approx(\bQ\tilde{\bU})\bsigma\bV^T\), truncated to rank \(k\) if required.



The algorithm touches \(\bA\) only through the two products \(\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) and \(\bQ^T\bA\). For a dense matrix these cost \(O(mn(k+p))\) flops, and for a sparse matrix \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)(k+p))\). The QR factorization and the small SVD cost \(O((m+n)(k+p)^2)\). The approximation error is \(\|\bA-\bQ\bQ^T\bA\|\), because \(\bQ\tilde{\bU}\bsigma\bV^T=\bQ\bQ^T\bA\). Halko, Martinsson, and Tropp prove that \[
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}\,\|\bA-\bQ\bQ^T\bA\|_F
    \leq\Big(1+\frac{k}{p-1}\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2\Big)^{1/2}
\end{align}
\] for Gaussian \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) (Halko et al. 2011). The second factor is the error of the truncated SVD, so the randomized method loses at most the first factor in expectation. With \(p=k+1\), that factor is \(\sqrt2\).






TipRemark



(Slowly decaying singular values) When the singular values decay slowly, the range of \(\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) contains significant components from the trailing singular vectors. Replacing \(\bY=\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) by \(\bY=(\bA\bA^T)^q\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) multiplies the \(j\)th singular direction by \(\sigma_j^{2q+1}\) and suppresses the trailing directions, exactly as in power iteration (the referenced result). In floating-point arithmetic, the columns are orthonormalized after each multiplication, because the powers otherwise become numerically dependent (Halko et al. 2011).

title: 28  Randomized Methods in Linear Algebra
text:
28.3 Random Sampling in Gaussian Elimination
the referenced section showed that eliminating a vertex joins all of its neighbors into a clique, and that the resulting fill makes sparse Cholesky expensive on large meshes. For the Laplacian of a weighted graph, the clique has an explicit form. Random sampling can replace it by a sparse graph that is correct on average.






NoteProposition: Elimination in a Graph Laplacian



Let \(\bL=\bD-\bW\) be the Laplacian of a connected graph with nonnegative edge weights \(w_{ij}\) and degrees \(d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}\). Eliminating vertex \(v\) produces a Schur complement that is again a graph Laplacian. Its graph is the graph of \(\bL\) with \(v\) removed, plus an edge of weight \(w_{iv}w_{jv}/d_v\) between each pair of neighbors \(i,j\) of \(v\).








TipProof





The Schur complement is \(\bS=\bB-\br\br^T/d_v\), where \(r_i=-w_{iv}\) and \(\bB\) is \(\bL\) with row and column \(v\) removed. For \(i\neq j\), \(s_{ij}=-w_{ij}-w_{iv}w_{jv}/d_v\), which is the negative of the stated edge weight. Every row of \(\bL\) sums to zero, so row \(i\) of \(\bB\) sums to \(w_{iv}\). Row \(i\) of \(\br\br^T/d_v\) sums to \(w_{iv}\sum_jw_{jv}/d_v=w_{iv}\). Hence every row of \(\bS\) sums to zero, and \(\bS\) has nonpositive off-diagonal entries, which characterizes a graph Laplacian.









NoteProposition: An Unbiased Sparse Replacement for the Clique



Let vertex \(v\) have neighbors \(1,...,\delta\) with weights \(w_i=w_{iv}\) and \(d=\sum_iw_i\). For each neighbor \(i\), draw one neighbor \(j\) with probability \(w_j/d\) and, if \(j\neq i\), add an edge between \(i\) and \(j\) with weight \(w_i/2\). The Laplacian of the resulting graph of at most \(\delta\) edges has expected value equal to the Laplacian of the clique in the referenced result.








TipProof





Let \(\bL_{ij}=(\be_i-\be_j)(\be_i-\be_j)^T\) be the Laplacian of a single unit edge, with \(\bL_{ii}=\bzero\). The expected Laplacian of the edge added for neighbor \(i\) is \(\sum_j(w_j/d)(w_i/2)\bL_{ij}\). Summing over \(i\) counts each unordered pair twice, so the expectation is \(\sum_{i<j}(w_iw_j/d)\bL_{ij}\), which is the Laplacian of the clique.



Eliminating every vertex in this way produces a factor \(\tilde{\bL}\) whose number of nonzero entries is proportional to the number of edges, rather than the superlinear fill of exact elimination. The factor is too inaccurate to solve with directly, but \(\tilde{\bL}\tilde{\bL}^T\) approximates \(\bL\) well enough to serve as a preconditioner for the conjugate gradient method of the referenced section. Kyng and Sachdeva use a refinement of this sampling, eliminate the vertices in random order, and prove that the resulting solver reaches relative accuracy \(\varepsilon\) in \(O(m\log^3n\log(1/\varepsilon))\) expected time for a graph with \(m\) edges (Kyng and Sachdeva 2016). Practical implementations eliminate vertices in minimum-degree order, which reduces fill further but is not covered by the proof.

title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.1 Initial Value Problems and Well-Posedness
An ordinary differential equation specifies the instantaneous velocity of a continuous state trajectory. A numerical time-stepping method replaces this continuous flow by a sequence of computable discrete states. The core mathematical questions in numerical ODE integration are consistency, zero-stability, global convergence, stiffness, and geometric structure preservation.

title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.3 Euler Methods and Stability Functions






NoteDefinition: Forward Euler, Backward Euler, and Trapezoidal Methods



For time step \(h = t_{n+1} - t_n\):

Forward Euler (explicit): \(\by_{n+1} = \by_n + h \boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by_n)\).
Backward Euler (implicit): \(\by_{n+1} = \by_n + h \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1})\).
Trapezoidal Rule (implicit Crank–Nicolson): \[
\begin{align}
\by_{n+1} = \by_n + \frac{h}{2} \left[ \boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by_n) + \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1}) \right].
\end{align}
\]









NoteTheorem: Stability Functions for Linear Test Equations



Applied to the Dahlquist test equation \(y' = \lambda y\) with \(z = h\lambda \in \fC\), the numerical update satisfies \(y_{n+1} = R(z) y_n\). The stability functions are: \[
\begin{align}
R_{\mathrm{FE}}(z) = 1 + z, \qquad
    R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}, \qquad
    R_{\mathrm{TR}}(z) = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2}.
\end{align}
\] The region of absolute stability is \(\mathcal{S} = \{z \in \fC : |R(z)| \leq 1\}\). Backward Euler and the Trapezoidal Rule are A-stable: \(\fC^- = \{z \in \fC : \operatorname{Re}(z) \leq 0\} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\). Backward Euler is additionally L-stable: \(\lim_{z \to -\infty} R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z) = 0\).








TipProof





For Forward Euler: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n = (1 + z)y_n\). For Backward Euler: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + z y_{n+1} \implies (1 - z)y_{n+1} = y_n \implies y_{n+1} = \frac{1}{1 - z} y_n\). For Trapezoidal Rule: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{z}{2}(y_n + y_{n+1}) \implies (1 - z/2)y_{n+1} = (1 + z/2)y_n \implies y_{n+1} = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2} y_n\). Let \(z = x + iy\) with \(x \leq 0\). For Backward Euler, \(|1 - z|^2 = (1 - x)^2 + y^2 \geq 1 + y^2 \geq 1\), so \(|R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z)| = \frac{1}{|1 - z|} \leq 1\). For Trapezoidal Rule, \[
\begin{align}
|1 + z/2|^2 = (1 + x/2)^2 + (y/2)^2 = 1 + x + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{4}, \\
    |1 - z/2|^2 = (1 - x/2)^2 + (y/2)^2 = 1 - x + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{4}.
\end{align}
\] Because \(x \leq 0\), we have \(1 + x \leq 1 - x\), which implies \(|1 + z/2|^2 \leq |1 - z/2|^2\) and \(|R_{\mathrm{TR}}(z)| \leq 1\). Thus both methods are A-stable. Along the negative real axis, \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} |R_{\mathrm{BE}}(x)| = \lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{1}{1 - x} = 0\), proving L-stability. In contrast, \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} R_{\mathrm{TR}}(x) = -1\), so the Trapezoidal Rule is not L-stable.

title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.4 Runge–Kutta Methods
Runge–Kutta methods achieve high orders of accuracy without storing historical steps by evaluating intermediate stages within each time step.






NoteDefinition: Classical Fourth-Order Runge–Kutta Method (RK4)



For an autonomous ODE \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(\by)\), the classical RK4 method computes four stages: \[
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol{k}_1 &= \boldsymbol{f}(\by_n), \\
    \boldsymbol{k}_2 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + \frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{k}_1 \right), \\
    \boldsymbol{k}_3 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + \frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{k}_2 \right), \\
    \boldsymbol{k}_4 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + h\boldsymbol{k}_3 \right),
\end{align}
\] and sets the update \[
\begin{align}
\by_{n+1} = \by_n + \frac{h}{6} \left( \boldsymbol{k}_1 + 2\boldsymbol{k}_2 + 2\boldsymbol{k}_3 + \boldsymbol{k}_4 \right).
\end{align}
\] The one-step defect is \(O(h^5)\). With the normalization in the referenced result, the local truncation error and the global error are both \(O(h^4)\).








NoteTheorem: RK4 Stability Polynomial



Applied to the scalar linear test equation \(y' = \lambda y\), the stability function of RK4 is \[
\begin{align}
R(z) = 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24} = \sum_{k=0}^4 \frac{z^k}{k!}, \qquad z = h\lambda.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Substituting \(f(y) = \lambda y\) into the RK4 stages: \[
\begin{align}
k_1 &= \lambda y_n, \\
    k_2 &= \lambda \left( y_n + \frac{h}{2} k_1 \right) = \lambda \left( 1 + \frac{z}{2} \right) y_n, \\
    k_3 &= \lambda \left( y_n + \frac{h}{2} k_2 \right) = \lambda \left( 1 + \frac{z}{2} + \frac{z^2}{4} \right) y_n, \\
    k_4 &= \lambda \left( y_n + h k_3 \right) = \lambda \left( 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{4} \right) y_n.
\end{align}
\] Substituting these into the update formula: \[
\begin{align}
y_{n+1} &= y_n + \frac{h}{6} \left[ \lambda + 2\lambda\left(1 + \frac{z}{2}\right) + 2\lambda\left(1 + \frac{z}{2} + \frac{z^2}{4}\right) + \lambda\left(1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{4}\right) \right] y_n \\
    &= y_n + \frac{z}{6} \left[ 1 + (2 + z) + \left(2 + z + \frac{z^2}{2}\right) + \left(1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{4}\right) \right] y_n \\
    &= y_n + \frac{z}{6} \left[ 6 + 3z + z^2 + \frac{z^3}{4} \right] y_n \\
    &= \left( 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24} \right) y_n.
\end{align}
\]

29.6 Exercises






WarningExercise




Derive. The discrete Gronwall lemma and Forward Euler convergence.

Let \(\by(t)\) solve \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(t, \by)\) with \(\|\boldsymbol{f}(t, \bu) - \boldsymbol{f}(t, \bv)\| \leq L\|\bu - \bv\|\). Use Taylor’s theorem to show that the one-step defect of Forward Euler satisfies \(\|\by(t_{n+1}) - (\by(t_n) + h\boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by(t_n)))\| \leq \frac{h^2}{2} M_2\), where \(M_2 = \max \|\by''(t)\|\).
Derive the error recurrence \(\|\be_{n+1}\| \leq (1 + Lh)\|\be_n\| + \frac{h^2}{2}M_2\).
Apply the referenced result to establish the rigorous global error bound \(\|\be_n\| \leq \frac{M_2}{2L}(e^{L(t_n - t_0)} - 1)h\).

Derive. A-stability and L-stability of implicit methods.

Plot the boundary of the Forward Euler stability region \(|1 + z| = 1\) in the complex plane. Show that for real \(\lambda < 0\), stability requires \(h \leq 2/|\lambda|\).
For the implicit Trapezoidal Rule, prove that \(|R_{\mathrm{TR}}(z)| = 1\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Re}(z) = 0\). Explain why this implies that undamped physical oscillations are integrated without artificial numerical dissipation.
Apply the Trapezoidal Rule and Backward Euler to the stiff problem \(y' = -1000y\), \(y(0) = 1\) with \(h = 0.1\). Show that Trapezoidal Rule produces oscillatory values \((-99/101)^n \approx (-0.98)^n\), whereas Backward Euler dampens the mode immediately to \((1/101)^n \approx 10^{-2n}\).

Explore. Symplectic geometry of the harmonic oscillator. Consider the harmonic oscillator \(q' = v\), \(v' = -q\) with exact energy \(E(q, v) = \frac{1}{2}(q^2 + v^2)\).

Compute the one-step update matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{FE}}\) for Forward Euler and show that \(\det(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{FE}}) = 1 + h^2 > 1\).
Compute the one-step update matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Verlet}}\) for Velocity Verlet. Confirm that \(\det(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Verlet}}) = 1\).
Show that Velocity Verlet conserves an exact modified shadow Hamiltonian \(\tilde{H}(q, v) = \frac{1}{2}(q^2 + v^2) - \frac{h^2}{4}q^2 = H(q, v) + O(h^2)\).

Compute. Adaptive step size control via embedded Runge–Kutta pairs.

An embedded pair computes a lower-order approximation \(\by_{n+1}^{[p]}\) and a higher-order approximation \(\by_{n+1}^{[p+1]}\) sharing stages. Show that the difference \(\be_{n+1} = \by_{n+1}^{[p+1]} - \by_{n+1}^{[p]}\) satisfies \(\|\be_{n+1}\| = C h^{p+1} + O(h^{p+2})\).
Given error tolerance \(\varepsilon\) and current step size \(h_{\mathrm{old}}\), derive the optimal step size formula \(h_{\mathrm{new}} = s h_{\mathrm{old}} (\varepsilon / \|\be_{n+1}\|)^{1/(p+1)}\) with safety factor \(s \in (0, 1)\).
Explain why adaptive solvers reject a step and repeat with smaller \(h\) when \(\|\be_{n+1}\| > \varepsilon\), and why step growth is capped by \(h_{\mathrm{new}} \leq 5 h_{\mathrm{old}}\) in production codes.

Explore. Stiffness in chemical cascades and BDF methods. Consider the singularly perturbed initial value problem \(\varepsilon y' = -y + \cos(t)\) with \(y(0) = 0\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-4}\).

Find the exact solution and identify the fast boundary layer transient \(e^{-t/\varepsilon}\) and the slow quasi-steady state \(\cos(t) + \varepsilon \sin(t)\).
Explain why explicit RK4 requires \(h \lesssim 2.8 \times 10^{-4}\) throughout the entire simulation, even after the transient has decayed to zero.
Formulate the BDF2 update \(\frac{3\by_{n+1} - 4\by_n + \by_{n-1}}{2h} = \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1})\) and show that it allows time steps \(h = 0.1\) in the smooth regime.










NoteFurther reading



Hairer, N{}rsett, and Wanner give a careful account of ODE methods and their analysis (Hairer et al. 1993). Dahlquist’s paper is the classical source for the stability barrier for linear multistep methods (Dahlquist 1963). Quarteroni, Sacco, and Saleri provide a broader numerical-analysis reference (Quarteroni et al. 2007).

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.1 Definitions and Preprocessing
(Running example: data matrices) Least squares used the data matrix to predict a response. PCA uses the same matrix to find the orthogonal directions along which the observations vary most. The SVD answers both questions.

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
NoteDefinition: Data Centering



Data matrix \(\bX \in \fR^{n\times p}\) (\(n\) samples, \(p\) features) must be centered: \[
\begin{align}
X_{ij} \leftarrow X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j, \quad \bar{x}_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}.
\end{align}
\] Throughout this section, \(\bX\) is assumed centered.








NoteDefinition: Sample Covariance Matrix



The matrix \(\bS = \frac{1}{n-1}\bX^T\bX \in \fR^{p\times p}\).

Diagonal: \(S_{jj}\) is the variance of feature \(j\).
Off-diagonal: \(S_{ij}\) is the covariance between features \(i\) and \(j\).
Property: \(\bS\) is symmetric positive semidefinite (SPSD).









WarningExercise



Derive.

Show that centering makes each column of \(\bX\) have mean zero.
Prove that the diagonal entries of \(\bS\) are sample variances.
Prove that \(\bS\) is symmetric positive semidefinite by computing \(\bz^T\bS\bz\).

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.2 PCA via SVD






NoteTheorem: Principal Directions and Scores



Let \(\bX = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\) be the SVD of the centered data matrix.

Principal Directions (Loadings): Columns of \(\bV\) (eigenvectors of \(\bS\)).
Principal Components (Scores): \(\bZ = \bX\bV = \bU\bsigma\).
Variances: \(\lambda_i = \text{Var}(\bz_i) = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}\).









TipProof





Substituting the SVD \(\bX = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\) into the sample covariance matrix \(\bS\): \[
\begin{align}
\bS &= \frac{1}{n-1} \bX^T\bX \\
    &= \frac{1}{n-1} \left( \bV\bsigma^T\bU^T \right) \left( \bU\bsigma\bV^T \right) \\
    &= \frac{1}{n-1} \bV \bsigma^T (\bU^T\bU) \bsigma \bV^T \\
    &= \bV \left( \frac{\bsigma^2}{n-1} \right) \bV^T.
\end{align}
\] Because \(\bV\) is orthogonal and \(\frac{\bsigma^2}{n-1}\) is diagonal with non-negative entries \(\frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}\), this is the spectral decomposition of \(\bS\). The columns \(\bv_i\) are eigenvectors of \(\bS\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2 / (n-1)\). The principal component score matrix is \[
\begin{align}
\bZ = \bX\bV = \left( \bU\bsigma\bV^T \right) \bV = \bU\bsigma (\bV^T\bV) = \bU\bsigma.
\end{align}
\] The sample covariance matrix of the scores is \[
\begin{align}
\bS_{\bZ} = \frac{1}{n-1} \bZ^T\bZ = \frac{1}{n-1} (\bsigma\bU^T)(\bU\bsigma) = \frac{\bsigma^2}{n-1} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_p),
\end{align}
\] confirming that distinct score columns \(\bz_i, \bz_j\) have sample covariance zero for \(i \neq j\).









TipRemark



(PCA stability) Forming \(\bX^T\bX\) squares the 2-norm condition number: \(\kappa_2(\bX^T\bX)=\kappa_2(\bX)^2\) when \(\bX\) has full column rank. Compute the singular vectors directly from an SVD when small singular values or numerical rank matter.








WarningExercise



Derive.

Starting from \(\bX=\bU\bsigma\bV^T\), compute \(\bS=(n-1)^{-1}\bX^T\bX\).
Show that the columns of \(\bV\) are eigenvectors of \(\bS\).
Show that the corresponding eigenvalues are \(\lambda_i=\sigma_i^2/(n-1)\).
Compute the score matrix \(\bZ=\bX\bV\) and prove that \(\operatorname{Cov}(\bZ)\) is diagonal.
Use the referenced result to explain the stability warning above.

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.3 Variance and Dimensionality Reduction






NoteDefinition: Proportion of Variance Explained (PVE)



For the first \(k\) components: \[
\begin{align}
\text{PVE}_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^p \sigma_i^2}.
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Optimal Approximation



The rank-\(k\) matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bX_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i \bu_i \bv_i^T
\end{align}
\] is the optimal \(k\)-dimensional linear approximation of the data in the Frobenius norm, by the Eckart–Young theorem.








WarningExercise



Derive.

Use the referenced result to prove the referenced result.
Show that \(\|\bX-\bX_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2\).
Show that \(\text{PVE}_k=1-\|\bX-\bX_k\|_F^2/\|\bX\|_F^2\).
Explain why a PVE threshold is a modeling choice, not a theorem.

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.4 Implementation Details






TipRemark



(Standardization) If features have different units, PCA will be dominated by large-scale features. Standardize by dividing each centered column by its standard deviation: \(X_{ij} \leftarrow (X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)/s_j\).








TipRemark



(Interpretation) Principal components are directions of large variance. A large loading identifies a direction of variation in the data matrix. It does not by itself explain why that variation occurs.








NoteDefinition: Dual PCA for \(p \gg n\)



When the number of features greatly exceeds the number of samples, we may diagonalize the \(n\times n\) Gram matrix \(\mathbf{K}=\bX\bX^T\) instead of the \(p\times p\) covariance matrix. For each nonzero singular value, the feature-space principal direction is recovered from \(\bv_i=\bX^T\bu_i/\sigma_i\). Kernel PCA replaces this linear Gram matrix by a centered nonlinear kernel matrix.

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.1 Graph Matrices and the Laplacian
Graph algorithms translate into numerical linear algebra once edge weights and vertex degrees are assembled into matrices. Undirected graphs lead to symmetric positive semidefinite Laplacians whose spectra characterize connectivity and graph cuts. Random walks and diffusion maps generalize these spectra to nonlinear manifold learning, offering multiscale geometric filtering and permutation-invariant representations for physical systems.
crumbs: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
NoteDefinition: Adjacency and Degree Matrices



For a weighted undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(n\) vertices:

Adjacency \(\bA\): \(A_{ij} = w_{ij} \geq 0\) if \((i,j) \in E\), and \(A_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. We assume \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\) and \(A_{ii} = 0\).
Degree \(\bD\): Diagonal matrix with entries \(D_{ii} = d_i = \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}\).









NoteDefinition: Unnormalized Graph Laplacian



The unnormalized graph Laplacian is \[
\begin{align}
\bL = \bD - \bA.
\end{align}
\] For any signal \(\bx \in \fR^n\) on the vertices, the action of \(\bL\) acts as a discrete Laplace operator: \[
\begin{align}
(\bL \bx)_i = \sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j).
\end{align}
\] The associated quadratic form satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\bx^T \bL \bx = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2.
\end{align}
\]








NoteProposition: Laplacian Positive Semidefinite



For an undirected graph with nonnegative weights, \(\bL\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and \(\bL\mathbf{1}=\bzero\).








TipProof





Symmetry follows from \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\), so \(\bA = \bA^T\) and \(\bL = \bD - \bA = \bL^T\). Expanding the quadratic form algebraically from definitions: \[
\begin{align}
\bx^T \bL \bx &= \bx^T (\bD - \bA) \bx = \sum_{i=1}^n d_i x_i^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij} \right) x_i^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\
    &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_j^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\
    &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2.
\end{align}
\] Because \(w_{ij} \geq 0\) and \((x_i - x_j)^2 \geq 0\), each term is non-negative, so \(\bx^T \bL \bx \geq 0\) for all \(\bx \in \fR^n\), proving positive semidefiniteness. For \(\bx = \mathbf{1}\), every coordinate satisfies \((\bL\mathbf{1})_i = d_i - \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij} = 0\), so \(\bL\mathbf{1} = \bzero\).









NoteTheorem: Spectral Properties of the Graph Laplacian



Let the eigenvalues of \(\bL\) be ordered as \(0 = \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq ... \leq \lambda_n\).

\(\lambda_1 = 0\) with eigenvector \(\bv_1 = \mathbf{1}\).
The multiplicity of eigenvalue \(0\) equals the number of connected components of \(G\).
The second smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\) is the algebraic connectivity (Fiedler value). It satisfies \(\lambda_2 > 0\) if and only if \(G\) is connected.









TipProof





the referenced result shows that all eigenvalues of \(\bL\) are nonnegative and that \(\mathbf{1}\in\ker(\bL)\), so \(\lambda_1=0\).
It remains to identify the entire nullspace. If \(\bx\in\ker(\bL)\), then \[
\begin{align}
0=\bx^T\bL\bx=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2.
\end{align}
\] Every term is nonnegative. Hence \(x_i=x_j\) across every edge with positive weight, and therefore \(\bx\) is constant on each connected component. Conversely, a vector that is constant on each connected component has zero difference across every edge and belongs to \(\ker(\bL)\). The indicator vectors of the connected components form a basis for this nullspace, so the multiplicity of eigenvalue zero equals the number of components.
In particular, \(G\) is connected exactly when \(\ker(\bL)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}\}\). In that case zero is a simple eigenvalue, so \(\lambda_2>0\). If \(G\) is disconnected, the nullspace has dimension at least two and \(\lambda_2=0\).









NoteCorollary: Rayleigh Characterization of Algebraic Connectivity



For a connected undirected graph, \[
\begin{align}
\lambda_2
    =\min_{\bx\perp\mathbf{1},\,\bx\neq\bzero}
    \frac{\bx^T\bL\bx}{\bx^T\bx}
    =\min_{\bx\perp\mathbf{1},\,\bx\neq\bzero}
    \frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2}{\sum_i x_i^2}.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





By the referenced result, a connected graph has an orthonormal eigenbasis with \(\bq_1=\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{n}\) and \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\). If \(\bx\perp\mathbf{1}\), then \(\bx=\sum_{k=2}^n c_k\bq_k\), and \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\bx^T\bL\bx}{\bx^T\bx}
    =\frac{\sum_{k=2}^n\lambda_k c_k^2}{\sum_{k=2}^n c_k^2}
    \geq\lambda_2.
\end{align}
\] Equality holds for a Fiedler eigenvector \(\bq_2\). The second expression follows from the referenced result.









NoteDefinition: Normalized Laplacians



Normalized Laplacians account for high-degree vertices:

Symmetric Normalized Laplacian: \(\bL_{\text{sym}} = \bD^{-1/2} \bL \bD^{-1/2} = \bI - \bD^{-1/2} \bA \bD^{-1/2}\). Its spectrum lies in the interval \([0, 2]\).
Random Walk Laplacian: \(\bL_{\text{rw}} = \bD^{-1} \bL = \bI - \bD^{-1} \bA\). It is similar to \(\bL_{\text{sym}}\) and shares its eigenvalues.

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.2 Spectral Clustering






NoteTheorem: Spectral Relaxation of Graph Cuts



Partitioning a graph into two disjoint sets \(A\) and \(B\) to minimize the normalized cut is NP-hard. Relaxing the discrete indicator vector to a continuous vector subject to an orthogonality constraint yields the Rayleigh quotient problem \[
\begin{align}
\min_{\bx \perp \bD\mathbf{1},\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bL \bx}{\bx^T \bD \bx}.
\end{align}
\] The optimal solution is the Fiedler eigenvector \(\bv_2\) of the generalized eigenvalue problem \(\bL \bv = \lambda \bD \bv\), or equivalently the second eigenvector of \(\bL_{\text{rw}}\). Spectral clustering embeds vertices in \(\fR^k\) using the first \(k\) nontrivial eigenvectors, then partitions the coordinates using \(k\)-means.

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.4 Permutation Invariance and Graph Spectra






TipRemark



(Combinatorial bottleneck in coordinate representations) In molecular systems and particle clusters with \(N\) identical atoms, the state is specified by atomic positions in \(\fR^{3N}\). Comparing two configurations \(\bx, \by \in \fR^{3N}\) directly requires optimizing over all \(N!\) atomic index permutations \(\sigma \in S_N\), in addition to Euclidean rotations and translations. This combinatorial alignment cost is intractable for moderate \(N\).








NoteTheorem: Permutation Invariance of Graph Spectra



Let \(\bD \in \fR^{N \times N}\) be the pairwise interatomic distance matrix with entries \(D_{ij} = \|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\|_2\). Under any atom permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\), the distance matrix transforms by an orthogonal permutation matrix \(\bP_\sigma\): \[
\begin{align}
\bD_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bD \bP_\sigma^T.
\end{align}
\] Let \(\bL\) be any graph Laplacian constructed from edge weights \(w_{ij} = f(D_{ij})\). Then the permuted Laplacian is \[
\begin{align}
\bL_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T.
\end{align}
\] Because \(\bP_\sigma\) is orthogonal, \(\bL_\sigma\) is orthogonally similar to \(\bL\). Therefore, the eigenvalue spectrum \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{spec}(\bL) = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, ..., \lambda_N)
\end{align}
\] is invariant under all atomic permutations \(\sigma \in S_N\) and all rigid Euclidean isometries \(\mathrm{SE}(3)\).








TipProof





Because rigid rotations and translations preserve pairwise distances \(\|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\|_2\), the matrix \(\bD\) is invariant under \(\mathrm{SE}(3)\).
Under a permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\), vertex \(i\) maps to \(\sigma(i)\), so the permuted affinity matrix has entries \(W_{\sigma(i), \sigma(j)} = W_{ij}\). In matrix notation, \(\bW_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bW \bP_\sigma^T\). Similarly, the degree matrix transforms as \(\bD_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bD \bP_\sigma^T\). Thus \[
\begin{align}
\bL_\sigma = \bD_\sigma - \bW_\sigma = \bP_\sigma (\bD - \bW) \bP_\sigma^T = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T.
\end{align}
\] Because permutation matrices are orthogonal (\(\bP_\sigma^{-1} = \bP_\sigma^T\)), the characteristic polynomial satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\det(\bL_\sigma - \lambda \bI)
    =
    \det(\bP_\sigma (\bL - \lambda \bI) \bP_\sigma^T)
    =
    \det(\bP_\sigma)\det(\bL - \lambda \bI)\det(\bP_\sigma^T)
    =
    \det(\bL - \lambda \bI).
\end{align}
\] The roots of the characteristic polynomial are identical. Thus the eigenvalue multiset \(\operatorname{spec}(\bL)\) is invariant under any relabeling of identical particles.
crumbs: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.5 Bandwidth Selection via Affinity Scaling






TipRemark



(Sigmoidal behavior of the affinity sum) The Gaussian affinity kernel \(K_{ij} = \exp(-\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2 / (2\delta^2))\) requires selecting the bandwidth parameter \(\delta\). If \(\delta\) is too small, points are isolated and \(K_{ij} \approx 0\) for \(i \neq j\). If \(\delta\) is too large, points are fully connected and \(K_{ij} \approx 1\).
Define the total affinity sum \[
\begin{align}
S(\delta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N \exp\left(-\frac{\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2}{2\delta^2}\right).
\end{align}
\] Plotting \(\ln S(\delta)\) against \(\ln \delta\) yields a sigmoidal curve:

As \(\delta \to 0\), \(K_{ij} \to 0\) for \(i \neq j\), so \(S(\delta) \to N\) and \(\ln S(\delta) \to \ln N\).
As \(\delta \to \infty\), \(K_{ij} \to 1\) for all \(i,j\), so \(S(\delta) \to N^2\) and \(\ln S(\delta) \to 2\ln N\).
In the intermediate scaling regime, \(S(\delta) \propto \delta^d\), where \(d\) is the intrinsic manifold dimension. The slope \(\frac{d\ln S(\delta)}{d\ln \delta} \approx d\) estimates dimension.

Choosing \(\delta\) in the linear transition regime ensures that the kernel resolves intrinsic manifold geometry without collapsing into disconnected points or a uniform complete graph.

31.6 Exercises






WarningExercise




Compute. (Path graph Laplacian spectrum) For a three-node unweighted path graph \(1-2-3\), write down \(\bA\) and \(\bL\). Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\bL\) by hand. Verify that \(\lambda_1 = 0\) with \(\bv_1 = (1, 1, 1)^T\), and compute the algebraic connectivity \(\lambda_2\).
Derive. (Rayleigh quotient for algebraic connectivity) For the path graph in the preceding exercise, minimize the quotient in the referenced result over vectors of the form \((a,b,-a-b)^T\). Verify that the minimum equals the computed value of \(\lambda_2\). Then evaluate the numerator on a two-level vector that is constant on each side of a proposed cut and explain how weak cross-cut weights lower its energy.
Derive. (Permutation invariance of graph spectra) Consider a cluster of four identical atoms in \(\fR^3\).

Let the coordinates be arranged in a vector \(\bx \in \fR^{12}\). Explain why comparing two configurations \(\bx\) and \(\by\) requires testing \(4! = 24\) permutations.
Construct the interatomic distance matrix \(\bD\) and form the graph Laplacian \(\bL\). Prove that for any permutation \(\sigma \in S_4\), \(\bL_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T\).
Explain how sorting the eigenvalues \(\operatorname{spec}(\bL) = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \lambda_4)\) produces a coordinate-free, permutation-invariant fingerprint for molecular structure.

Explore. (Diffusion time as a geometric low-pass filter) Let a diffusion operator on a data manifold have leading eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 0.98\) and \(\lambda_2 = 0.80\).

Compute the ratio of modal contributions \((\lambda_2 / \lambda_1)^{2t}\) for diffusion times \(t = 1\), \(t = 5\), and \(t = 20\).
Explain why increasing \(t\) contracts local high-frequency fluctuations while preserving macroscopic manifold geometry.
What happens to the diffusion distance \(D_t(\bx_i, \bx_j)\) as \(t \to \infty\)?

Explore. (Sigmoidal bandwidth selection) Let \(N = 100\) data points be sampled uniformly from a circle of radius \(R = 1\) in \(\fR^2\).

Write down the formula for the affinity sum \(S(\delta) = \sum_{i,j} \exp(-\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2 / (2\delta^2))\).
Evaluate the asymptotic limits of \(\ln S(\delta)\) as \(\delta \to 0\) and \(\delta \to \infty\).
In the intermediate scaling regime \(\delta \in [0.1, 0.5]\), show that the slope \(\frac{d\ln S(\delta)}{d\ln \delta} \approx 1\), reflecting the one-dimensional geometry of the circle.










NoteFurther reading



Chung develops spectral graph theory from the graph-Laplacian side (Chung 1997). Belkin and Niyogi introduce Laplacian eigenmaps, while Coifman and Lafon develop diffusion maps and the density normalization described above (Belkin and Niyogi 2003; Coifman and Lafon 2006).

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
32.1 Definition, Properties, and the Sparse Bottleneck
(Running example: Markov chains) A probability vector governed by a finite-state generator satisfies \(\bp(t)=e^{t\bA}\bp_0\). The exponential action developed here advances that distribution without forming \(e^{t\bA}\). The next chapter adds positivity, conservation, and truncation structure.
Linear evolution equations describe continuous physical and probabilistic processes throughout scientific computing. Consider the autonomous initial-value problem $$ \[\begin{align}

    \frac{d\bu}{dt} = \bA\bu(t), \qquad \bu(0) = \bv,
\end{align}\] \[
where $\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}$ or $\fC^{n \times n}$ is an infinitesimal generator or spatial discretization matrix, and $\bv$ is a prescribed initial state. The analytical solution is given by the matrix exponential action
\] \[\begin{align}

    \bu(t) = e^{t\bA}\bv.
\end{align}\] $$ When \(n\) is large and \(\bA\) is sparse, computing the full matrix \(e^{t\bA}\) is computationally prohibitive. We evaluate the vector action \(e^{t\bA}\bv\) directly through projection onto Krylov subspaces.
crumbs: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
NoteDefinition: The Matrix Exponential



For any square matrix \(\bA \in \fC^{n \times n}\), the matrix exponential is defined by the convergent power series \[
\begin{align}
e^{\bA} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\bA^k}{k!} = \bI + \bA + \frac{1}{2}\bA^2 + \frac{1}{6}\bA^3 + ...
\end{align}
\] For any scalar \(t \in \fR\), the matrix function \(e^{t\bA}\) satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt} e^{t\bA} = \bA e^{t\bA} = e^{t\bA}\bA\).








NoteTheorem: Algebraic Properties of the Matrix Exponential



Let \(\bA, \bB \in \fC^{n \times n}\).

If \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) commute (\(\bA\bB = \bB\bA\)), then \(e^{\bA+\bB} = e^\bA e^\bB\). If they do not commute, this equality fails in general.
The matrix exponential is always nonsingular, with inverse \((e^\bA)^{-1} = e^{-\bA}\).
For any nonsingular similarity transform \(\bS\), \(e^{\bS\bA\bS^{-1}} = \bS e^\bA \bS^{-1}\). In particular, if \(\bA = \bQ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bQ^{-1}\) is diagonalizable, then \(e^\bA = \bQ \operatorname{diag}(e^{\lambda_1}, ..., e^{\lambda_n}) \bQ^{-1}\).
The determinant satisfies Jacobi’s formula: \(\det(e^\bA) = e^{\operatorname{trace}(\bA)}\).









TipProof





Property (1) follows by expanding the Cauchy product of the series for \(e^\bA\) and \(e^\bB\), where commutativity permits the binomial theorem for \((\bA+\bB)^k\). Property (2) is a direct consequence of (1) with \(\bB = -\bA\), since \(\bA\) commutes with \(-\bA\) and \(e^{\bzero} = \bI\). Property (3) follows from \((\bS\bA\bS^{-1})^k = \bS\bA^k\bS^{-1}\). Property (4) follows from the Schur decomposition \(\bA = \bQ\bT\bQ^*\): the diagonal entries of \(\bT\) are the eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\), the diagonal entries of \(e^\bT\) are \(e^{\lambda_i}\), and the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries: \(\det(e^\bA) = \det(e^\bT) = \prod_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda_i} = e^{\sum \lambda_i} = e^{\operatorname{trace}(\bA)}\).









TipRemark



(Dense evaluation vs. the vector action bottleneck) Classical methods for computing the full \(n \times n\) matrix \(e^{\bA}\) rely on scaling and squaring with rational Padé approximants. Evaluating an \([m/m]\) Padé approximant requires computing matrix powers and solving matrix linear systems, incurring \(O(n^3)\) operations. More critically, even when \(\bA\) is sparse, the exponential \(e^{t\bA}\) is typically dense. Storing \(e^{t\bA}\) for \(n = 10^6\) requires eight terabytes of memory in double precision. Many evolution calculations require only the action \(e^{t\bA}\bv\), which can be approximated without forming the full exponential.

text:
32.4 Shared Krylov Spaces and Quadrature
To evaluate the bilinear integral numerically, we approximate both paths using independent forward and adjoint Krylov spaces, and integrate the contraction using Gauss–Legendre quadrature.






NoteTheorem: Bilinear Quadrature Evaluation



Let \(\mathcal{K}_{m_f}(\bA, \bv)\) have basis \(\bV_f\) and projected Hessenberg matrix \(\bH_f\), with \(\beta_f = \|\bv\|_2\). Let \(\mathcal{K}_{m_a}(\bA^*, \nabla_{\by}\ell)\) have basis \(\bV_a\) and projected matrix \(\bH_a\), with \(\beta_a = \|\nabla_{\by}\ell\|_2\). At any Gauss–Legendre node \(s_q \in [0, 1]\) with quadrature weight \(w_q\), the path approximations are \[
\begin{align}
\bm{f}^{(q)} = \beta_f \bV_f e^{s_q h \bH_f}\be_1, \qquad \blambda^{(q)} = \beta_a \bV_a e^{(1-s_q) h \bH_a}\be_1.
\end{align}
\] The coefficient gradient evaluates to \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta_j} \approx h \sum_{q=1}^{n_q} w_q \operatorname{Re}\left[ (\blambda^{(q)})^* \bA_j \bm{f}^{(q)} \right].
\end{align}
\]








TipRemark



(One-sided termination in refinement heuristics) A common stopping diagnostic tests the product of forward and adjoint residuals \(\rho_f \rho_a\). If the forward path reaches an invariant subspace, \(\rho_f = 0\), causing the product to vanish even when the adjoint path is at depth \(m_a = 2\) and completely unresolved. Reliable stopping criteria require monitoring forward and adjoint convergence separately.

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
section: 32.5 Generator Recovery via the Matrix Logarithm
text:
32.5 Generator Recovery via the Matrix Logarithm
When discrete-time snapshot maps \(\bK_h \approx e^{h\calA}\) are observed rather than continuous trajectories, we invert the exponential map using the principal matrix logarithm.






NoteDefinition: The Matrix Logarithm



Let \(\bK \in \fC^{n \times n}\) have no eigenvalues on the closed negative real axis \((-\infty, 0]\). The principal matrix logarithm \(\log(\bK)\) is the unique matrix \(\bA\) such that \(e^\bA = \bK\) and all eigenvalues of \(\bA\) satisfy \(|\operatorname{Im}(\lambda)| < \pi\).








TipRemark



(Projection and finite-time closure bias) If \(P\) denotes the orthogonal projection onto a subspace of observables \(\calF\), the projected generator obtained from finite-time observations satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bA}_h = h^{-1}\log\left( P e^{h\calA} |_{\calF} \right) \neq P\calA|_{\calF}.
\end{align}
\] Unless \(\calF\) is invariant under \(\calA\), projection and exponentiation do not commute. The resulting finite-time closure bias can be expanded in powers of \(h\), but its leading order depends on which terms leave the observable space. Any rate such as \(O(h^r)\) therefore requires a separately defined closure depth and corresponding assumptions.

text:
32.6 Exercises






WarningExercise




Compute. Dense vs. Action Complexity: A sparse matrix \(\bA \in \fR^{10^6 \times 10^6}\) has 10 nonzero entries per row. Compute the memory required to store \(e^{h\bA}\) as a dense array. Compare this with storing \(m=30\) Arnoldi basis vectors.
Compute. Adjoint Sharing: Let an overcomplete library contain \(M_{\mathrm{lib}} = 200\) candidate directions. Calculate the number of sparse matrix–vector products needed to evaluate all 200 coefficient gradients using (a) directional Fréchet derivatives and (b) the adjoint Krylov formula with 5 quadrature nodes.
Check. Logarithm Branch Cuts: Let an evolution operator have oscillatory eigenvalue \(\lambda = -\gamma + i\omega\) with \(\omega = 50\pi\). Determine the maximum observation interval \(h\) that avoids branch-cut crossing in the principal matrix logarithm.
Explore. Taylor vs. Krylov Convergence: For the 1D discrete Laplacian \(\bA\) with \(\|\bA\|_2 = 4 \times 10^4\) and \(t = 10^{-2}\), compare the polynomial degrees suggested by a direct Taylor remainder bound and by Krylov projection. State every estimate you use, since neither degree is determined by \(\|\bA\|_2\) alone.
Explore. One-Sided Termination: Construct a \(3 \times 3\) example where \(\bv\) is an exact eigenvector of \(\bA\), yielding forward residual \(\rho_f = 0\) at step 1, while the adjoint starting vector is not an eigenvector. Explain why product heuristics fail in this setting.









NoteFurther reading



Higham gives the general theory of matrix functions (Higham 2008). Moler and Van Loan explain why apparently reasonable methods for the matrix exponential can fail, and Al-Mohy and Higham develop a modern action method that avoids forming the exponential (Moler and Van Loan 2003; Al-Mohy and Higham 2011).

title: 33  Markov Chains, Continuous Generators, and the CME

33.1 Discrete-Time Markov Chains
(Running example: Markov chains) In this setting the entries of the exponential action are transition probabilities and its column sums preserve total mass. Consequently, the probability mass that leaks out of a truncated state space is an observable measure of the truncation error.
Markov chains model random systems where transitions depend only on the current state. Discrete-time systems evolve via column-stochastic matrices \(\bx^{(k+1)}=\bP\bx^{(k)}\). Continuous-time Markov jump processes evolve via infinitesimal generators \(\dot{\bp}(t)=\bA\bp(t)\), leading to the Chemical Master Equation. Large or infinite state spaces require projection onto finite subgenerators with rigorous 1-norm leakage bounds.

title: 33  Markov Chains, Continuous Generators, and the CME
text:
NoteDefinition: Probability Vector



A vector \(\bx\in\fR^n\) is a probability vector if \[
\begin{align}
x_i\geq 0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1.
\end{align}
\] The entry \(x_i\) represents the probability of occupying state \(i\).








NoteDefinition: Column-Stochastic Matrix



A matrix \(\bP \in \fR^{n \times n}\) is column-stochastic if:

\(P_{ij} \geq 0\) for all \(i,j\).
\(\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij} = 1\) for each column \(j\).









TipRemark



(Column convention) Column \(j\) of \(\bP\) contains the transition probabilities from state \(j\) to all destination states \(i\). The update rule for a probability distribution is \(\bx^{(k+1)} = \bP \bx^{(k)}\).








NoteTheorem: Spectrum of a Stochastic Matrix



If \(\bP\) is column-stochastic, then \(\lambda=1\) is an eigenvalue, and every eigenvalue satisfies \(|\lambda|\leq 1\).








TipProof





The column sum condition implies \(\mathbf{1}^T\bP=\mathbf{1}^T\). Thus \(\lambda=1\) is a left eigenvalue with eigenvector \(\mathbf{1}^T\), which guarantees that \(1\) is an eigenvalue of \(\bP\).
To bound the spectral radius, let \(\bP^T\bv=\lambda\bv\) with \(\bv\neq \bzero\). Choose index \(j\) such that \(|v_j| = \|\bv\|_\infty = \max_i |v_i|\). Taking the \(j\)-th component of the eigenvalue equation yields \[
\begin{align}
|\lambda|\,|v_j|
    =
    \left|\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}v_i\right|
    \leq
    \sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}|v_i|
    \leq
    \left(\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}\right) |v_j|
    =
    |v_j|.
\end{align}
\] Dividing by \(|v_j|>0\) gives \(|\lambda|\leq 1\).









NoteDefinition: Stationary Distribution



A probability vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is stationary if \(\bP \boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\). It is a right eigenvector of \(\bP\) associated with \(\lambda=1\), normalized so that \(\mathbf{1}^T\boldsymbol{\pi}=1\).








NoteTheorem: Perron–Frobenius for Markov Chains



If \(\bP\) is irreducible (every state can be reached from any other state in finitely many steps) and primitive (aperiodic, so \(\bP^k > 0\) elementwise for some \(k \geq 1\)), then:

\(\lambda_1 = 1\) is an algebraically and geometrically simple eigenvalue.
\(|\lambda_i| < 1\) for all other eigenvalues \(\lambda_i \neq 1\).
The stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is strictly positive in every entry.
For any initial probability vector \(\bx^{(0)}\), \(\lim_{k\to\infty} \bP^k \bx^{(0)} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\).









NoteDefinition: Spectral Gap and Mixing Time



For a primitive chain with eigenvalues ordered as \(1 = \lambda_1 > |\lambda_2| \geq ... \geq |\lambda_n|\), the spectral gap is \[
\begin{align}
\delta = 1 - |\lambda_2|.
\end{align}
\] For a diagonalizable matrix, the error \(\|\bx^{(k)} - \boldsymbol{\pi}\|_2\) decays asymptotically as \(\mathcal{O}(|\lambda_2|^k)\). The number of steps \(k_\varepsilon\) required to reach error tolerance \(\varepsilon\) satisfies \[
\begin{align}
k_\varepsilon \approx \frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\delta}.
\end{align}
\]








NoteDefinition: Detailed Balance (Reversibility)



A Markov chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) if \[
\begin{align}
P_{ij} \pi_j = P_{ji} \pi_i \qquad \text{for all } i, j.
\end{align}
\] A chain satisfying detailed balance is reversible.








NoteTheorem: Real Spectrum of Reversible Chains



Let \(\bP\) satisfy detailed balance with stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi} > 0\). Define \(\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\pi})\). Then the matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bS = \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1/2} \bP \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{1/2}
\end{align}
\] is symmetric. Consequently, all eigenvalues of \(\bP\) are real, and \(\bP\) has an orthogonal basis of eigenvectors in the inner product weighted by \(\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1}\).








TipProof





The \((i,j)\) entry of \(\bS\) is \[
\begin{align}
S_{ij} = \pi_i^{-1/2} P_{ij} \pi_j^{1/2} = \frac{P_{ij}\pi_j}{\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j}}.
\end{align}
\] By detailed balance, \(P_{ij}\pi_j = P_{ji}\pi_i\). Substituting this equality gives \[
\begin{align}
S_{ij} = \frac{P_{ji}\pi_i}{\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j}} = \pi_j^{-1/2} P_{ji} \pi_i^{1/2} = S_{ji}.
\end{align}
\] Thus \(\bS = \bS^T\). Because \(\bP\) is similar to the real symmetric matrix \(\bS\), its eigenvalues are real.
